metadata.shortDescription:
Independence Title Tackles the Issue of Closing Real Estate Doubles on the Latest Episode of "Title Tuesdays" when it comes to real estate investing and how to wholesale real estate.

Leading title insurance company Independence Title's Kevin Tacher delivers his informed thoughts on Double Closings & Transactional Funding in a new video.

CONNECT WITH US HERE!
Facebook: https://goo.gl/u5lmCo
Instagram: https://goo.gl/jGnyEQ
Twitter: https://goo.gl/yQXSx5
Google+: https://goo.gl/n7V4rh

It's a truth in the title insurance world that many companies are frightened of double closings and avoid them like the plague.  Is there a good reason for this reluctance?  Not according to Independence Title and their founder, CEO, and best-selling real estate author Kevin Tacher who dives into the subject on episode #101 of his popular "Title Tuesdays".  In Tacher's eyes the issue is not a double or even triple closing, but the level of professionalism in which they are handled.  When dealt with by pros like Independence Title, double closings can be a complete win for all concerned.  Not shockingly, this eye-opening education is likely to be good news for many who find themselves considering a double closing as an attractive option.

"As long as it's made sure the closing happen separate from each other there's no problem legally or ethically with double closings,"  commented the always compelling Tacher. "The key is to make sure you have professionals working with you, like our own Independence Title, so no mistakes are made that could lead to later headaches.  Transactional Funding is a big part of the process to keep things legal.  Get in touch with us if you have any questions."

Independence Title is committed to never breaking any laws that could endanger their clients or their own license to operate.  There are some cases where, in unique cases, double closings are not permitted.  But a quick conversation with one of Independence Title's experts can make sure that the double, triple, or even quadruple closing goes through without any concern for the investor.

This video's information is confirmed by their happy clients.

Jason C., from Florida, recently said in a five-star review, "Independence Title handled a double closing for me no problem at all, and I turned a great profit.  A-plus service."

For more information watch the video at https://youtu.be/lLbfcHAX30o

Founded several years ago by Amazon.com Best-Selling Author Kevin Tacher, Independence Title Inc. is located in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

They are one of South Florida's fasting growing and most awarded Title Insurance Agencies.

Independence Title is locally owned and managed. Their team provides real estate professionals with attentive customer service, state of the art technology, mobile applications, and continued training. Together with the support of the top underwriters in the title insurance industry, they have the expertise to complete real estate transactions with the highest level of efficiency and client service.

Real Estate Investing - Double - Triple Closings with No Money!

Real estate investing has unique types of transactions that are not found in many other businesses.  One of the most important is the ability to complete transactions without the use of the Real Estate Investor's personal funds -- a no money deal using transactional funding .   Essentially these deals use no money, no credit and no risk on the Real Estate Investor's part.

Real estate investor transactions that require two or more closings are referred to as double closings because of the various "legs" of the transaction.  For example, the investor is usually referred to as the "B" Buyer and the original homeowner Seller is called the "A" leg in the first part of the transaction.  When the homeowner sells to the investor then the A -- B leg of the transaction will be completed.

This first leg of the real estate transaction is usually done within minutes of the second leg.  In this second part or leg, the investor (B) sells to the end-buyer who is designated as "C".  The no money part of the transaction comes into play if the investor can use the end-buyer's funds for his purchase to fund the A -- B transaction with the homeowner Seller.

Many closing agents and closing attorneys will not allow a Real Estate Investor to use the end-buyer's (C's) funds to do the A -- B closing leg.  The investor can ask the end-buyer to use his funds to close the A -- B leg so he will have no money in the transaction.  Sometimes this works but it can alert the end-buyer that the investor has a weakness and that is he may not be able to close, resulting in the Real Estate Investing deal not closing.

There are additional alternatives for real estate double - Triple closings when the end-buyer funds cannot be used.  The most used one is transactional funding where a lender loans the investor money for a few hours while the A --B leg and the B -- C leg close.  After these closings the transactional funder's money is wired back to him -- all in the same day.

Real estate investing using double closings is very lucrative and requires no money, no credit and no risk for real estate investors.  To the casual observer, it would seem impossible to buy a home or rental property with no money what-so-ever and be able to then sell it and make a profit.  This is because most homeowners are only familiar with borrowing money and getting a mortgage on their personal residence.  

When you learn real estate investing, you'll better understand how important real estate double closings actually are.  Even if you have tons of money, you should always strive to use as little of it as possible. In summary, real estate double closings are essential to every real estate investor's success.

metadata.title: Wholesaling In 2026: Double Closing, Transactional Funding & Protecting Your Spread | EP1
metadata.author: Closer Control
metadata.shortDescription:
Wholesaling is changing. Regulations are tightening, buyers are getting savvier, and if you are still relying on simple assignments, your 20K to 40K spreads are at risk.

In this episode of The Conner Rueca Show, Conner sits down with Peter Russell of Velocity Advantage Capital, a wholesaler turned transactional funding partner who has done 600 plus deals and hundreds of double closes. They break down exactly how real operators are protecting their profit as states move to regulate wholesaling.

This is not theory. It is how to keep your deals alive and your spreads intact.

In this episode you will learn:

-When to double close instead of assigning a contract
-How transactional funding actually works step by step
-How to structure A to B and B to C so buyers and sellers do not blow up your deal
-How to handle EMD, closing costs and title the smart way
-What to expect as more states regulate wholesaling in 2026
-Why regulation will wipe out the noise and reward the real operators

If you are wholesaling in a tight market or making big spreads, this is the playbook for not getting squeezed at the closing table.

segments.text: Hi there. If you're in real estate
investing, especially double closing,
you've probably heard the term
transactional funding. But what does it
actually mean and when should you use
it? Let's break it down in plain
English.
Transactional funding is a short-term
loan that helps you close a deal when
you don't have the cash upfront. Here's
how it works. You've got a property
under contract with the seller. That's
the A2B transaction. You've also lined
up an end buyer who's ready to purchase
from you. That's the B TOC transaction.
A transactional lender steps in and
funds the A2B closing. Then once your
end buyer closes on B TOC, the lender is
immediately paid back. All of this
usually happens on the same day or
within 24 hours.
So when does transactional funding make
sense? First, when assignments aren't
allowed, either by law by the seller or
by your title company. Second, when you
want to protect your wholesale profit so
your buyer doesn't see exactly what
you're making. And third, when you need
to show credibility at the closing table
by being the actual buyer of record.
Let me give you a quick example. You
contract a property for $100,000 with
the seller. You find an end buyer
willing to pay $115,000.
The lender provides the $100,000 for the
A2B transaction. You close with the
seller. Then immediately after you sell
to your end buyer for $115,000.
The lender takes their fee at closing
and you keep the difference. In this
case, your $15,000 spread minus the
lender's fee. Now, let's talk about
fees. Transactional funding isn't free.
Lenders usually charge 1 and a half to
3% of the funded amount or a flat fee.
The key thing to remember is that the
fee comes out at closing. You don't pay
it upfront. That means your spread must
be large enough to cover the fee and
still leave you with a profit. So, if
your fee ends up being $2,000 and your
spread is $15,000, you walk away with
13,000 at the end of the day. Here's
something a lot of beginners overlook.
Not all lenders are the same. Working
with an experienced transactional lender
can make the difference between a deal
falling apart and getting across the
finish line. At Fuel My Deal, we
navigate risks that come up during
double closes. We work directly with
title companies and attorneys who may
not always understand how transactional
funding works, and we help make sure
your deal closes smoothly, on time, and
without surprises. When you've got a
lender that knows what they're doing,
you can move forward with confidence and
focus on finding more deals.
Like any funding strategy, there are a
few risks. If your end buyer backs out,
you could be stuck. If timelines get
pushed, fees may increase. And not every
title company is double close friendly,
so partner with one that is.
Transactional funding is a powerful tool
when used strategically. It helps you
protect profits, stay compliant, and
close deals with confidence. Want to go
deeper? Download our free doubleclose
guide using the link in the description.
And if you've got a deal ready right
now, submit it at fueldeal.com and let's
get you funded.

If your end buyer backs out, you could be stuck. If timelines get pushed, fees may increase. And not every title company is double close friendly, so partner with one that is. Transactional funding is a powerful tool when used strategically. It helps you protect profits, stay compliant, and close deals with confidence. Want to go deeper? metadata.title: How to Get Double Close Funding for Your Wholesale Deals (FAST!)
metadata.author: Jasper Cool
metadata.shortDescription:
What is a double closing / transactional funding?
You’ll see how it works: first, you buy from the seller (A → B), then immediately resell to your buyer (B → C) — typically on the same day — all while the title company handles both closings.

Why many title companies demand funds up front
Even if the second sale happens right away, they often won’t accept that as “funding” for the first side. That’s where transactional funding comes in.

How Bright Closings funding works, step by step

Fill out our online funding request form

Provide all necessary deal details and signed contracts

We review (often in minutes)

We coordinate with your title or closing attorney

We fund the first closing (A → B) and then let the second closing (B → C) happen

Your profit (spread) and our fee are taken at closing — $0 out of your pocket

All the details you need to fill out the form
What name to use (your personal name vs LLC), property address, A → B purchase price, closing date, title company info, whether they know it’s a double close, and how to upload your A → B & B → C contracts.

Fees, states, and limits explained

Deals $75,000 or less → flat fee of $850

Deals over $75,000 → 1% of purchase price + $100 processing

Fee is paid from closing proceeds (i.e. you don’t bring money to the table)

We fund in 47 states (excluding New York, Alaska, Hawaii)

No credit checks, no income docs, no appraisals — all focus is on your deal, not your personal finances

Typical approval turnaround is extremely fast (often within 5–10 minutes)

How we handle title attorneys / closers
We reach out to them, explain the structure, get what’s required, and make sure they’re completely on board. So you don’t have to do all that legwork.

When and why this is critical

You’ve got a buyer locked in but no funds to close

You need to protect your reputation with sellers

You want deals to close on time, every time

You want a reliable funding instrument that works nationwide

Risks, legal considerations & best practices

Ensuring both closings happen on the same day

Title / escrow compliance

Knowing your state-specific rules (some states are stricter)

How to vet your title company or attorney to accept double closings

Always maintain transparency and legal structure (don’t “pretend” the first close doesn’t exist)

🔗 Links & Resources

✅ Get your deal funded now (BrightClosings.com form):
https://www.brightclosings.com/get-funding-now

ℹ️ Bright Closings – How It Works & FAQ:
https://www.brightclosings.com
 
Bright Closings

✉️ Email for support / questions: brightclosings@gmail.com

🛡 Why Investors Trust Bright Closings

$0 out of pocket required — no upfront cash needed

No credit checks, no appraisals, no income docs — we underwrite the deal, not the person 
Bright Closings

Fast turnaround — in many cases we respond within 5–10 minutes

Transparent pricing — flat fees or simple percentage + processing

Experienced team — we deal in wholesale & transactional funding all day, every day

Nationwide reach (except 3 states) — you can do business across the U.S. 
Bright Closings

💡 Pro Tips Before You Apply

Make sure your closing attorney or title company understands exactly what a double close is (some balk at it)

Have clean signed contracts (A → B and B → C) ready to upload

Use a title company you trust or have them on board early

Double-check all contact info (attorney, buyer, seller)

Time your submission — submit as early as possible on closing day

Don’t let funding be the reason a deal dies. Use Bright Closings to keep things smooth, professional, and profitable.

If you found this helpful, smash that Like button, hit Subscribe for more real estate finance strategies, and drop your questions in the comments — I'm happy to help.

See you on the bright side of funding. ✨

metadata.title: Assignment vs. Double Close: How Wholesalers Close Deals (Costs, Funding, Michigan Rules) | ORES 101
metadata.author: Odardo LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Assignment vs. double close, explained for beginners. In Episode 2 of ORES 101 (Odardo Real Estate School, lesson RE201-03), you'll learn the two main ways a wholesale deal closes, what each one costs, when buyers, title companies, and lenders prefer one over the other, how transactional funding works, why honesty and disclosure still matter, and what Michigan's broker law says.

In this lesson
- Assignment: you sell your rights in the purchase contract ("and/or assigns"). One closing, one deed, seller to end buyer. Your fee is usually paid on the closing statement.
- Double close: A sells to you (B), then you sell to C. Two closings, two deeds, often the same day.
- Transactional funding: a very short-term loan for the first leg of a double close.
- Costs: usually one set of closing costs vs. two. No dollar figures here: get an itemized estimate and verify every number with your title company.
- Lender rules: FHA requires buying from the owner of record with no sale or assignment of the contract, and resales within 90 days of the seller's purchase are generally ineligible (24 CFR 203.37a).
- Honesty: tell sellers you're an investor who may assign or resell. Never claim to be the end buyer if you're not.
- Michigan: MCL 339.2502b broker-license triggers. HB 5366 (proposed wholesaling and disclosure rules) is NOT law; as of Nov 16, 2026 it was introduced Dec 16, 2025 and referred to the House Committee on Government Operations. See a Michigan real estate attorney.

Chapters
0:00 Welcome to ORES 101, Episode 2
0:10 The question + learning goals
0:32 Key point 1: How an assignment works
1:09 Key point 2: How a double close works
1:49 Transactional funding
2:23 Key point 3: Costs (verify with your title company)
2:56 Key point 4: When buyers, title companies & lenders prefer one
3:53 Honesty & disclosure
4:27 Key point 5: Michigan note (MCL 339.2502b, HB 5366)
5:33 How to choose: 3 questions
6:02 Recap quiz
6:22 Quiz answers
6:39 Homework
6:54 Disclaimer
7:05 Next class: Ep03

Sources (checked Nov 16, 2026)
- MCL 339.2502b (Michigan Legislature): https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-339-2502b
- House Bill 5366 of 2025, bill status and history: https://legislature.mi.gov/Bills/Bill?ObjectName=2025-HB-5366
- FHA sale-of-property rule, 24 CFR 203.37a (eCFR): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-24/subtitle-B/chapter-II/subchapter-B/part-203/subpart-A/section-203.37a
- Michigan Consumer Protection Act, MCL 445.901 et seq.: https://legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=mcl-445-903
- Title company explainers on assignments, double closings, and transactional funding: https://georgiatitle.com/help/Real-Estate-Help/Wholesaling-Double-Closing-Assignments/index.html and https://www.aurumtitle.com/resources/wholesale-assignment-double-closing-title-texas/ (other states; rules differ, so ask a title company in your state)

Homework: call two title companies near you. Ask: Do you close assignments? Do you close double closes? How do you need each leg funded? Can I get an itemized cost estimate? Write the answers in your spreadsheet.

Quiz answers: (1) One closing. (2) A short-term loan for the first leg of a double close. (3) More than 5 sales in any 12-month period.

Series: Odardo Real Estate School (ORES) · ORES 101 · Episode 2 (RE201-03)
Next class: Episode 3, Is Wholesaling Legal in Your State? The Nationwide Picture

This video is for education only. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it is not a substitute for a licensed attorney, real estate agent or broker, CPA, or lender. Real estate laws differ by state, county, and city, and they change. Talk to a licensed professional in your state before you sign, market, or fund a deal.

segments.text: Welcome back to Odardo Real Estate
School. This is Ores 101 episode two,
assignment versus double close.
Here's the question. You've got a house
under contract and a cash buyer who
wants it. How do you actually close the
deal and get paid? There are two main
ways, an assignment or a double close.
By the end of this lesson, you'll be
able to explain how each one works, what
it costs, who prefers which, and how to
pick the right one for a deal honestly
and legally.
Key point one, the assignment. You sign
a purchase contract with the seller,
usually with your name followed by the
words and or assigns. Then you sign a
second document, an assignment agreement
with your cash buyer. That agreement
transfers your rights in the contract to
the buyer and it states your assignment
fee. Notice what you're selling, not the
house. You're selling your rights in the
contract. At closing, the seller deeds
the property straight to your buyer.
There's one closing and one deed and you
never go on title. Your fee is usually
paid by the title company on the closing
statement.
Key point two, the double close. Here,
you actually buy the property, then you
sell it. Picture three letters, A, B,
and C. A is the seller, B is you, and C
is your end buyer. First, A sells to
you. That's closing number one. Then you
sell to C. That's closing number two.
Each leg has its own contract, its own
closing statement, and its own deed. The
two closings are often on the same day,
sometimes back-to-back at the same title
company. For a short time, you are the
owner of record. Your profit is the
difference between your buying price and
your selling price minus your costs.
That raises a big question. In a double
close, where does the money for closing
number one come from? You have to pay
seller A in full. Some investors use
their own cash. Others use
funding, which is a very short-term loan
made just for the first leg of a double
close. Lenders that offer it usually
want to see your signed contract with
the end buyer, and they charge a fee.
Some title companies will not let you
use your buyer's money to pay for your
own purchase, so ask early how they
handle it and read the terms, including
what happens if the second closing gets
delayed.
Key point three, costs. An assignment
usually has one set of closing costs. A
double close has two closings, so it
usually has two sets, title work,
possibly title insurance on each leg,
recording fees, and possibly transfer
taxes on each deed. Add transactional
funding fees if you use them. I'm not
going to give you dollar figures because
they change by state, county, title
company, and deal. Get an itemized
estimate and verify every number with
your title company before you sign.
Key point [music] four, who prefers
which? Many wholesalers like an
assignment because it's simpler,
cheaper, [music] and you don't need
money to buy the house. But your fee
shows up on the closing statement, and
some buyers or sellers push back when
they see a big number. A double close
keeps the two prices on separate
statements, [music]
so some wholesalers choose it on larger
spreads if their title company allows
it. Some title companies are cautious
about same-day double closes. Title
companies differ, so call a few
investor-friendly ones and ask, do you
close assignments? Do you close double
closes? How must each leg be funded?
Also know the lender rules. Under the
federal FHA rule, a property bought with
an FHA loan must come from the owner of
record with no sale or assignment of the
contract, and resales within 90 days of
the seller's purchase generally aren't
eligible. That's why most wholesale
deals go to cash buyers or private
money.
Now, why honesty still matters. A double
close can keep your profit off the other
party's statement. Off a statement does
not mean secret, and it never means you
can mislead anyone. Deeds are public
records. Tell sellers upfront that
you're an investor and that you may
assign the contract or resell the
property. Never claim to be the end
buyer if you're not. Michigan's Consumer
Protection Act bans unfair or deceptive
practices. Use disclosure language your
attorney approves and get everything in
writing. Your reputation is your
business.
Key point five, the Michigan note.
Wholesaling is not banned in Michigan,
but the broker licensing law, MCL
says an owner selling real estate as a
principal vocation needs a broker
license unless they use a broker. It
lists four triggers, more than five
sales in any 12 months, telling the
public you're principally in the
business of selling real estate,
spending over half your working time or
more than 15 hours a week over six
months selling real estate, or being a
licensed salesperson selling property
other than your home. In a double close,
you actually own and resell the
property, so ask your attorney how that
counts toward those triggers. There's
also a proposed bill, House Bill 5366
that would add wholesaling and mandatory
disclosure rules. As of November 2026,
it had been introduced in December 2025,
referred to the Committee on Government
Operations, [music] and it is not law.
Check its status yourself and see a
Michigan real estate attorney before
your first deal.
So how do you choose? Ask three
questions. One, does my contract allow
assignment? If not, you may need a
double close or the seller's written
consent. Two, how is my buyer paying?
Cash buyers can usually do either.
Finance buyers often can do either
quickly, so check with their lender.
Three, what will my title company accept
and what will it cost? Get the answer in
writing, then pick the method that is
legal, affordable, and fully disclosed.
Recap quiz. Three questions. Pause the
video and answer them out loud. One, in
an assignment, how many closings are
there? Two, [music] what is
transactional funding used for?
in Michigan, how many sales in 12 months
is the line in the broker law?
Answers. [music] One, an assignment has
one closing and the seller deed straight
to your buyer. Two, transactional
funding is a short-term loan that pays
for the first leg of a double close.
Three, more than five sales in any
12-month period. How did you do?
Your homework. Call two title companies
near you. Ask them, do you close
assignments? Do you close double closes?
How do you need each leg funded? And can
you give me an itemized cost estimate?
Write their answers in your spreadsheet.
This lesson is for education only. It is
not legal, tax, or financial advice.
Laws differ by state. Talk to a licensed
professional before you act.
Next class, [music]
episode three. Is wholesaling legal in
your state? We'll look at the nationwide
picture and how to check your own
state's rules in three steps. Subscribe
to Odardo LLC so you don't miss it.

Wholesaling is changing fast across the country.

Title companies are tightening policies, states are starting to regulate assignment fees, and deals that used to close easily are now getting questioned—or completely blown up at the closing table.

In this episode of The Closers Club, David Olds sits down with Peter Russell to break down one of the most important strategies wholesalers need to understand right now: double closings.

Instead of exposing your assignment fee to buyers and sellers, a double closing allows you to purchase the property and resell it the same day—keeping both transactions separate and protecting your profit.

Peter also explains how his team at Velocity Capital helps wholesalers nationwide fund the A-to-B purchase, allowing them to immediately resell the property to their end buyer—sometimes within hours.

If you’ve ever had a buyer question your assignment fee or a title company refuse to close your deal, this episode might save your next paycheck.

metadata.title: Why the Gator Method Is a Great Way to Get Started in Real Estate
metadata.author: Pace Morby
metadata.shortDescription:
In today’s video, Pace Morby breaks down why the Gator Method is one of the greatest ways to get started in real estate investing. He explains each way private money lenders, also known as Gators, make money through different transaction scenarios. Wholesalers need earnest money and double closing funding, fix-and-flip and BRRRR investors need purchase price money, rehab money, and other private money, and who can provide that money? Gators! They can also act as private money partners (PMPs) that provide money and get equity of a deal in exchange!

He also discusses what Gators get access to upon joining the community: corporate credit training, access to capital, and even access to Pace’s capital! Gators don’t have to cold call, pull lists, follow up with buyers and sellers, or have any sales experience. Pace emphasizes that SubTo students FIND the deals and Gators FUND the deals.

metadata.shortDescription:
Transactional funding, earnest money deposit (EMD) funding, double closes, and creative finance strategies are powerful tools real estate investors use to close deals without using their own money. In this episode of Fund My Deal, Jose sits down with transactional lender Mandy Carna to explain how wholesalers and investors use transactional funding to secure deals, fund earnest money deposits, and complete double close transactions.

If you're a wholesaler, creative finance investor, or real estate entrepreneur, understanding how transactional funding works can help you close more deals, scale faster, and leverage other people’s money.

In this episode, Mandy explains:

How transactional funding works for real estate deals
How wholesalers can use earnest money deposit (EMD) funding to secure contracts
The difference between transactional funding, gap funding, and bridge loans
How to structure double close real estate transactions correctly
How the stack method (seller carryback stacking) allows investors to acquire properties creatively
Why having the right title company, lender, and team is critical for closing deals

Mandy also shares real deal stories, including:

A successful stack method deal where an investor acquired a property with none of their own money
A costly mistake where a title company mishandled a double close transaction and forced a wholesaler to lose half of a six-figure assignment fee

If you're trying to break into real estate investing, wholesaling, or creative finance deals, this episode will help you understand how funding partners can help you close deals and grow your business.

If you want to follow or invest with Mandy you can reach her at:

Beginner & advanced wholesalers

end buyer, often within hours. This is

the lender, plus a small fee. You never
hold the property long-term, and you're
not using your own cash, just leverage
and timing. So, why use transactional

deals where assignment isn't allowed. It
protects your profit margins by keeping
the original purchase price private. And
it gives you credibility. You're
actually buying the property before
reselling it. Even better, there are no
credit checks, no income requirements,

price. Of course, it's not free. Most

What is Transactional Funding?
Transactional funding is a short-term loan that is borrowed and paid back quickly, usually within the same day, and sometimes as long as a week. Access to this kind of short-term financing allows real estate wholesalers to buy and resell properties quickly without using any of their own money.
Transactional funding is almost exclusively used to wholesale properties through the double close method. It gives real estate investors the cash they need to buy a property from a home seller and allows the real estate investor to resell it for a profit in a separate transaction.

Why Would a Real Estate Wholesaler Used Transactional Funding?
Real Estate transactional funding serves as a replacement for when assigning contacts isn’t permitted. Such as wholesaling bank REO properties or if you do not want to disclose how much profit you are making to the seller and buyer. 
When it’s not possible to assign a contract or if you choose not too, investors may then turn to transactional lending to complete a wholesale deal. As a result, transactional lending enables investors to conduct legal back-to-back closings in a matter of days, if not hours.  This is how Paul and I have wholesaled REO properties in 44 states. 
While transactional funding has proven invaluable to seasoned wholesalers, there’s one caveat: transactional funding for real estate wholesale deals usually requires an end buyer to be lined up prior to receiving funds. A transactional lender will typically require borrowers to have already found a subsequent buyer for the property. 
If you know the wholesale property is a deal but don’t have a buyer lined up or if you are selling to a conventional loan buyer and they won’t be ready for another month then you want to close with a non-transactional loan.  Such as a private lender or hard money lender and not a transactional lender. 

How Does Transactional Funding Work?
Transactional funding is only used when there is an established end buyer in place. This end buyer should be ready to buy the subject property from the real estate wholesaler immediately after the wholesaler purchases the property from the original seller, and the sale proceeds from the end buyer are used to pay back the transactional funding loan. 

Transactional funding can be used with any type of real estate, provided the closing agent is willing to facilitate both transactions and the lender can verify all the important details before dispersing the funds.

Here’s how transactional funding works:
- The wholesaler/investor finds a seller and both parties agree to a below-market purchase price (the A-to-B transaction).
- When the wholesaler/investor finds an end-buyer, they will sign a new purchase agreement (the B-to-C transaction) to purchase the property at a higher price and close on the same day as the A-to-B transaction. 
- The wholesaler/investor secures transactional funding to buy the property from the seller.
When both transactions are complete, the wholesaler/investor repays the transactional funding loan from the proceeds of the B-to-C transaction and keeps the difference as their profit.

For example:  If a real estate wholesaler gets a property under contract at $100,000 and then finds an end-buyer that will purchase the property for $120,000.  The wholesaler reaches out to a transactional lender and the transactional will review the deal.  If all is OK, the transactional lender will lend $100,000 plus closing costs for the wholesaler to purchase the property. Then the same day or next day, the end-buyer purchases purchase the property for $120,000.  The transactional lender will receive $100,000 plus their fee. The wholesaler will receive $20,000 minus closing costs minus transactional lender fee.

metadata.title: Earnest Money Deposit (EMD): Where It Goes and What Happens If You Cancel
metadata.author: Katie Anderson | PENSACOLA AREA REALTOR ®
metadata.shortDescription:
Earnest money is a deposit held in escrow by the title company or closing attorney named in the contract. It isn’t paid directly to the Realtor or seller. If the sale closes, the deposit is credited toward the buyer’s purchase price.

If a contract is canceled, who receives the deposit depends on the contract terms, the cancellation deadline, and the circumstances. If the buyer and seller disagree about its release, the funds may remain in escrow until they reach an agreement or the dispute is resolved.

In this video, I explain how EMD works and walk through common examples involving inspection and appraisal timelines in Northwest Florida. Your signed contract controls what applies to your transaction.

Buying or selling in the Pensacola area?
Katie Anderson, Realtor | Keller Williams Realty Gulf Coast
Call or text: 850-324-3510
https://www.katieandersonrealestate.com/

metadata.title: Setting up a Real Estate Joint Venture
metadata.author: Clint Coons Esq. | Real Estate Asset Protection
metadata.shortDescription:
The typical joint venture goes something like this: Investor approaches GAP FUNDING PARTNER and presents the investment opportunity and offers the GAP FUNDING PARTNER a portion of the profits when the property sells (sometimes this includes interest).  The Investor will be in control of the project and will obtain a loan from the HARD MONEY LENDER.  To memorialize the deal the Investor will present the GAP FUNDING PARTNER with a real estate joint venture agreement that explains the overall deal.  Herein is where problems sometimes begin to arise.

Problem #1 – When investor attempts to borrow from HARD MONEY LENDER he is asked for proof of funds i.e., where did he get the money for the down payment.  When HARD MONEY LENDER learns, the funds are coming from GAP FUNDING PARTNER, HARD MONEY LENDER requires GAP FUNDING PARTNER to go on the loan.

Problem#2 – GAP FUNDING PARTNER is reluctant to go on the loan because GAP FUNDING PARTNER is not on title.  Typically title is held in Investor’s LLC or corporation so GAP FUNDING PARTNER is asked to take on full financial liability without any direct ownership.

Problem #3 – HARD MONEY LENDER will not allow Investor to give GAP FUNDING PARTNER a second deed of trust for his investment into the deal.

Problem #4 – GAP FUNDING PARTNER is typically in the dark as to what is happening with the project and if the project goes off track GAP FUNDING PARTNER will not find out until it is too late and HARD MONEY LENDER is foreclosing.

Problem #5 – Opposite of #4 because GAP FUNDING PARTNER decides to pull out of the project and will not commit to fully funding.  The investor is then left in the position of not being able to complete the project.

To solve these issues dispense with the joint venture agreement and create a joint venture limited liability company.  The JV LLC solves all of the aforementioned problems as follows:
Problem #1 – Funds are no longer an issue for HARD MONEY LENDER because Investor and GAP FUNDING PARTNER are members in the JV LLC that is purchasing the property.

Problem #2 – GAP FUNDING PARTNER is willing to go on the loan because GAP FUNDING PARTNER is an owner in the property through the JV LLC.

Problem #3 – No longer need a 2nd deed of trust because GAP FUNDING PARTNER is an owner i.e., he has security.

Problem #4 – GAP FUNDING PARTNER will be part of the decision-making process because he is a manager in the JV LLC and he is on the loan so he will get an immediate notice from HARD MONEY LENDER if a payment is missed or the project is not on track.

Problem #5 – Investor has less risk of GAP FUNDING PARTNER pulling out of the deal because if GAP FUNDING PARTNER puts the project in jeopardy he is personally liable on the loan.

metadata.author: True Title

segments.text: ala settlement
statement the Ala settlement statement
is the statement of accounting for the
closing it reflects all money's Changing
Hands payments being made closing
credits debits or other
adjustments if your closing includes a
loan you should note that the Ala
contains all of the information that may
also be shown on the lender's closing
disclosure as you review this document
and listen to the recording please note
page totals may vary based on the
specific nature of your
transaction the first page of the Ala
contains a summary of the transaction
the title company information is at the
top and then the property address buyer
or seller or borrower information and
loan information if any appear in the
next
box after the basic information the
accounting Begins the Ala is broken into
sections
the financial section will reflect the
sale price of the property earnest money
deposit loan amount and possibly other
credits or debits made in connection
with the sale
contract the prorations and adjustments
section will include the items being
adjusted at closing such as property
taxes homeowners association assessment
sewer assessments and so forth the loan
charges section identifies all of the
charges specific to the loan and payable
to the mortgage lender items such as an
origination fee prepaid interest and so
on the other loan charges section
includes items which were required by
the lender but which are paid to outside
parties such as the appraisal flood
certification and credit
report the impound section includes
items being held in escrow for the
mortgage property taxes homeowners
insurance and other assessments paid on
an ual basis it may also include an
aggregate adjustment which is a credit
given from the lender back to the buyer
based on a calculation made required
under mortgage lending
regulations the title charges in escrow
and settlement charges section contains
all of the charges collected by the
title company in association with the
closing for missoury properties please
note that the title insurance premium
and closing protection fee have been
calculated according to rates filed with
the Missouri Department of Insurance
financial institutions and professional
registration however Title service
charges closing charges and other fees
are not limited by state law the
government recording and transfer
charges section will include the charges
levied by the county for recording the
deed mortgage and other documents
required in connection with the
closing the miscellaneous section is a
catchall for any other other items being
paid at closing commonly including items
such as the survey invoice homeowners
insurance attorney's fees and so
on all of the amounts shown in the above
section are then subtotal in the debit
and credit columns and the next line
will include an amount due from meaning
you must pay it for
closing after your review please sign
and date on the signature page
[Music]

metadata.title: Title vs Escrow: What's the Difference? (Explained Simply)
metadata.author: Propy
metadata.shortDescription:
What's the difference between title and escrow? Title is about the house: is it really theirs to sell, and is it clean? Escrow is about the money: holding it safely until everyone has done their part. And the word escrow actually means two different things.

Eric from Propy explains what title and escrow each do, how they work together step by step, and what changes in Florida, Arizona and Colorado.

👉 Learn more about Propy Title: https://propy.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=title_vs_escrow&utm_content=top

CHAPTERS
0:00 Title vs escrow: the short answer
0:42 Part 1: What title really means
1:24 Two title insurance policies (only one protects you)
1:58 Part 2: What escrow does
2:48 Escrow means two different things
3:13 Part 3: How title and escrow work together
4:25 Part 4: Florida, Arizona, Colorado
5:30 Recap
5:54 Why close with Propy

TITLE VS ESCROW IN ONE MINUTE
Title: your legal right to own the home. The title company searches public records (past owners, old mortgages, unpaid taxes, liens, judgments), clears any problems and issues title insurance. About 36% of transactions need extensive work to clear title before closing (ALTA, 2024).
Escrow: a neutral third party that holds the money and documents and releases nothing until every condition in the contract is met.
Title is the investigator. Escrow is the referee.

TWO TITLE INSURANCE POLICIES
Lender's policy: protects the lender's loan.
Owner's policy: protects you, the buyer, if a covered problem from before you bought shows up later. It's a one time payment at closing.

TWO KINDS OF ESCROW
Closing escrow: holds the deal's money until closing.
Mortgage escrow account: set up by your lender after closing to pay property taxes and homeowners insurance from your monthly payment.

BY STATE
Florida: the title company usually acts as both closing agent and escrow agent. Title insurance premiums are set by state rule; other fees can differ. Who pays for the owner's policy depends on the county.
Arizona: escrow agents are licensed by the state, separately from title agents, and the purchase contract works as the escrow instructions.
Colorado: title companies commonly handle the closing, the contract sets a deadline for the title commitment, and title companies file their closing fees with the state.
Alabama: Propy closings are handled by Delta South Title, powered by Propy.

WHY CLOSE WITH PROPY
Propy Title is a title and escrow company serving Florida, Arizona, Colorado and Alabama, built to make closing fast, secure and simple.
Faster: escrow opens 24/7, Propy's earnest money record is 4 minutes, and Propy's AI helps catch contract issues early.
More secure: your deposit is paid inside the Propy platform, wiring instructions are verified on every closing, and every signer's identity is verified.
Smoother: one platform, one live status, and Avery, Propy's AI Escrow Officer, keeps everyone updated.
Rated 5.0 out of 5 on Google from 300+ reviews.

FAQ
What is the difference between title and escrow?
Title is about ownership of the house; the title company proves it's clean and insures it. Escrow is about the money; a neutral party holds funds and documents until every condition is met.

Do I need both a title company and an escrow company?
Usually not. In most deals, one title company handles both jobs.

Who protects me as the buyer?
The owner's title policy. The lender's policy only protects the lender.

Sources: ALTA Curative Work Study, 2024; CFPB; Florida Administrative Code 69O-186; Arizona DIFI, A.R.S. 6-813; Colorado Division of Insurance.

ABOUT PROPY
Propy is a vertical AI for autonomous closing infrastructure for real estate. With licensed title and escrow operations powered by AI and smart contracts, Propy's platform automates the entire real estate closing process, from offer to deed recording, allowing transactions to occur 24/7 with fewer intermediaries, less paperwork and higher security. In doing so, Propy is removing inefficiencies with outdated legacy systems and removing cost barriers that prevent access to real estate.

metadata.title: Credit Card Stacking for Real Estate Investors: The Same-Day Stack Nobody Explains Right
metadata.author: Gap Funding | 100% Real Estate Financing
metadata.shortDescription:
Most videos tell you to get a 0% card, use it for rehab, pay it off. Nobody explains what actually determines whether you get approved for $50,000 or $150,000 at 0% for 12 to 18 months.

It's not which card you pick. It's how the applications go in.

In this video:

→ Why submitting applications on the same day beats spacing them out, and how spacing actually kills your stack
→ Why your location and existing banking relationships decide which cards you should actually apply for, not which ones have the best rewards
→ The double stack: layering personal 0% cards alongside your business stack for more capacity, and the exact rule for when NOT to do it
→ How to turn approved credit into actual usable cash for down payments, closing costs, and contractor invoices
→ A real $50K stack walked through start to finish, from application to deal exit
→ How to grow your stack bigger after every single deal you close

The difference between a $50,000 stack and a $150,000 one isn't the card. It's the strategy.

📋 Book a free funding review (soft pull, no hard credit check, 2 mins) → https://gapfunded.com/apply

🏗️ Set up your LLC via Doola → https://partnersps.doola.com/gap

🏦 Hard money loans via Kiavi → https://try.kiavi.com/gap

💳 Liquidate credit limits into cash via Plastiq → https://www.plastiq.com

💰 Move credit into your account as cash via Kashu → https://signup.kashupay.com?referrer=wvBwa0NK357vBQ

⏱ TIMESTAMPS
0:00 – Why most credit stacking advice misses the part that actually matters
1:00 – Why same-day beats sequenced applications
1:45 – Why location and banking relationships decide which cards to apply for
2:35 – The double stack: business and personal cards at the same time
3:45 – Plastiq vs Kashu: turning credit into actual usable cash
4:30 – A real $50K stack, start to finish
5:25 – The one thing that breaks this entire strategy
6:05 – The bottom line
6:30 – Bonus: growing your limits after every deal exit

🚧🚧🚧 DISCLAIMER 🚧🚧🚧
Mick Wadley is not a CPA, attorney, insurance agent, contractor, lender, or financial advisor. The content in these videos shall not be construed as tax, legal, insurance, financial, or investment advice and may be outdated or inaccurate; it is your responsibility to verify all information yourself. This is a YouTube video for entertainment and educational purposes ONLY.

Apply to work with me one-on-one: https://www.cleartheshelf.com/apply

Apply for 0% interest credit cards here: https://www.cardratings.com/bestcards/business-credit-cards.php?src=704525

He was stuck at $30K a month for four months straight. Profitable, healthy sell-through, more leads than money to buy them. The problem wasn't sourcing. It was capital. So he got his first two credit cards, $110K combined, and within five months he hit his first $100K month. He's now done over $7M in Amazon sales in his early 20's.

Sadeq has built $385,000 in business credit lines across Chase, American Express, Capital One, and others. He walks us through the exact card stack, the application sequence, billing cycle optimization, the funding traps that cost sellers thousands, and why 0% APR credit cards are the single best scaling tool for OA sellers who've outgrown their cash.

Personal credit score of 700+

Emergency funding when you're already struggling

metadata.author: The Mortgage Man - Steve Ferguson
metadata.shortDescription:
Thinking about buying your next home before selling your current one?
A bridge loan could be your secret weapon. In this video, I’ll explain exactly what a bridge loan is, how it works, and how homeowners use bridge financing to buy first, sell later — without the stress of juggling two mortgages or missing out on your dream home.

🏠 You’ll learn:

What a bridge loan is and how it differs from traditional financing

When a bridge loan makes sense (and when it doesn’t)

The pros, cons, and real numbers you should know

How to qualify for a bridge loan

Real-world examples of how my clients used bridge loans successfully

Whether you’re moving up, relocating, or just tired of making offers contingent on selling your home, this video breaks down how to buy before you sell — step by step.

00:00 Introduction
00:36 What is a bridge loan?
00:57 Types of bridge loans
01:48 My favorite bridge loan
02:22 What bridge loan funds can be used for
02:41 What happens when you get a bridge loan?
03:43 Bridge loan fee
04:10 Bridge loan math example
06:16 Worse case scenario on the bridge loan
07:19 Loan programs you can use a bridge loan on
07:29 Bridge loan limitations/ property restrictions
08:48 Conclusion

segments.text: Hard money and bridge loans get mixed up all the time. Some people use the two names
as if they mean the same thing. They don't, and picking the wrong one can cost you a
deal.
In this presentation from Easy Lending USA, we'll break down what each loan is, how
much you can borrow, and how to tell which one fits the property in front of you.
Let's start with the big picture. Hard money isn't one specific loan. It's a family
of short-term loans from private lenders, sized mainly on the property and your
experience, not your tax returns.
The fix and flip loan covers the purchase and the renovation.
The bridge loan finances a property as it stands today, with no renovation budget.
Ground up construction loans fund a brand new build.
And multifamily bridge loans cover apartment buildings and mixed use property. So a
bridge loan is really one type of hard money loan. The real question is which type
fits your deal.
So what exactly is a bridge loan?
It's sized on what the property is worth today, based on an as is appraisal, not on
what it could be worth after a renovation.
There's no construction budget. The property is livable or rentable as it stands, or
very close to it.
The term is usually twelve to eighteen months. That's the bridge: time to sell,
lease it up, or line up long-term financing.
And it's built around your exit. The lender wants to see clearly how the loan gets
paid off, either by a sale or by a refinance.
Now let's put the two most common hard money loans side by side: the fix and flip
loan, and the bridge loan.
The biggest difference is how they're sized. A flip loan looks at your total cost
and the after repair value, or ARV for short. A bridge loan looks at the value
today.
For experienced investors, a flip loan can go up to ninety percent of cost, capped
at seventy-five percent of the ARV. A bridge loan tops out around seventy-five
percent of the current value.
A flip loan includes renovation money, released in draws as the work gets done. A
bridge loan doesn't fund repairs.
The term is about the same, twelve to eighteen months. And both can close quickly.
Seven to fifteen days from a complete file is typical.
Let's walk through an example. An investor finds a rent ready duplex listed at four
hundred thousand dollars. The seller wants to close in ten days, and there's a cash
buyer circling.
A conventional loan can't close that fast. So the investor uses a bridge loan.
At seventy-five percent of value, the bridge loan is three hundred thousand dollars.
That leaves about one hundred thousand of the investor's own cash, plus closing
costs.
Once the units are leased, the investor refinances into a long-term DSCR loan, which
qualifies on the rent. The bridge loan did its job: it won the deal.
So how do you decide? Start with the property itself.
If it needs real work, like a new kitchen, a roof, or a full gut, use a fix and flip
loan. That way the renovation is part of the financing.
If it's rent ready and the problem is speed, a bridge loan is simpler. Fewer moving
parts, no draws, no inspections.
Bridge loans also help when an existing loan is about to mature, and you need time
to sell or refinance.
And they let you buy your next property before the last one sells.
Now let's look at bridge loan leverage. Like most hard money, it depends on your
track record.
With two or more completed deals, many lenders go up to seventy-five percent of the
value, with a credit score of six-twenty or higher.
With one deal behind you, expect about seventy-two and a half percent.
And new investors can still get financed, typically up to seventy percent, with a
credit score of six-fifty or higher.
Loan sizes run from about one hundred fifteen thousand to eight million dollars. If
you're refinancing to pull cash out, the limit is usually lower, around sixty-five
percent.
If you're refinancing a property you already own, there's one rule that catches a
lot of investors. It's called seasoning.
If you've owned the property for more than twelve months, the bridge loan is usually
sized on the current appraised value.
If you've owned it for less than that, most lenders size it on your cost basis
instead. That's your purchase price plus the improvements you can document. So keep
every receipt and invoice.
Let's be balanced about it.
On the plus side, hard money and bridge loans close fast, they're sized on the
property and your experience, and there are no tax returns or income ratios to
document.
The trade-offs: rates are higher than a long-term mortgage, the term is short, and
you need a clear plan to pay the loan off. They're also for investment property
only, made to an LLC, never for a home you live in.
Here are four mistakes we see over and over.
One, using a bridge loan on a property that needs a big renovation. There's no rehab
money in a bridge loan, so all of that work comes out of your pocket.
Two, no clear exit. If you're selling, show recent comparable sales. If you're
keeping it, show the market rent and how it qualifies for a long-term loan.
Three, ignoring seasoning. Refinance too early and the loan may be sized on what you
paid, not what it's worth.
And four, treating short-term money like long-term debt. Line up your refinance or
your sale before you close, not in month eleven.
When you're ready to submit a deal, have these ready.
The property address and the purchase price or current value, a payoff statement if
you're refinancing, and a line by line rehab budget if there's work to do.
Then your exit plan with the numbers behind it, the deals you've completed in the
last three years, your LLC name, and your approximate credit range. A complete file
is what gets you a fast closing.
If you're not sure whether your deal needs a bridge loan or a fix and flip loan,
Easy Lending USA can look at it and match it with the right private lender.
There are no application or upfront fees to you. You can submit your deal at
easylendingusa.com, or call us at (858) 800-2280.
If this helped, subscribe for more plain English breakdowns of investor financing.
Thanks for watching, and we'll see you in the next one.

metadata.title: Ex-Big-Bank Lender Explains Bridge Loan Secrets in 6 Minutes
metadata.author: SEI Mortgage - Ryan Marks
metadata.shortDescription:
You're about to lose your dream home because you haven't sold your current one. But what if there's a way to buy now and sell later?

In this episode, Ryan Marks breaks down exactly how bridge loans work and how homeowners can use them to upgrade without the pressure of selling first.

WHAT IS A BRIDGE LOAN?
A bridge loan is a short-term loan that bridges the gap between selling your current home and buying your new one. It lets you:

✓ Buy your dream home NOW (don't lose it to another buyer)
✓ Leverage the equity in your current property
✓ Avoid the stress of selling under pressure
✓ Level up to your next home on YOUR timeline
✓ Skip the "contingent offer" that scares sellers

HOW BRIDGE LOANS WORK:
The lender calculates your loan based on:
- Value of your current home
- Value of your new home
- Outstanding loan balance on current property
- Maximum loan-to-value (LTV) is typically 75%

EXAMPLE FROM THE VIDEO:
• Current home value: $1,000,000 (no mortgage)
• New home value: $2,000,000
• Combined property value: $3,000,000
• Max loan available (75% LTV): $2,250,000

IDEAL FOR:
• Homeowners upgrading to a larger property
• Buyers who found their dream home and can't wait
• Anyone tired of selling first, then buying
• People with significant home equity
• Regular wage earners AND self-employed

WHO CAN GET A BRIDGE LOAN:
You don't need to be a real estate investor. Regular homeowners with equity in their current property can absolutely qualify.

KEY QUESTIONS TO ASK:
1. What's my maximum loan amount based on my equity?
2. What are the rates and fees?
3. How long is the bridge period?
4. What happens if my house doesn't sell?
5. Can I get both properties at the same time?

---

TIMESTAMPS:
0:00 - Hook: You're about to lose your dream home...
0:30 - What is a Bridge Loan? (Definition)
2:15 - How Bridge Loans Work (The Math)
4:00 - Bridge Loan Example: $1M → $2M Property
6:30 - Maximum Loan-to-Value (75% Rule)
8:00 - Who Can Get a Bridge Loan (Not Just Investors)
10:00 - Key Questions to Ask Your Lender
12:00 - When to Use a Bridge Loan (When it Makes Sense)
14:00 - Final Tips & Call to Action

---

Schedule a free consultation with Ryan Marks to discuss your specific situation and see if a bridge loan is right for you. Visit www.seimortgage.com

So what that means is if you have access to cash, let's say for example, you're going to take a home equity line of credit out on your existing property and use that money towards the down payment in order to buy your new home before selling your existing property, guess what? You have to qualify for the debt-to-income ratios not only on the new property, but also on the existing financing of that current property and whatever the payment's going to be on that home equity line of credit that you used for the down payment on your new home. So if you can't qualify to meet the debt-to-income ratios, it's very difficult for you to secure financing while you wait to sell that property using a HELOC method. However, a lot of the bridge loan products that we offer use no debt-to-income ratios whatsoever. More importantly, they also offer deferred payments. So it's a lot like a home equity line of credit where the investor's going to allow you to access the cash in your existing home in order to put the money down on the new loan, but you're going to essentially have one loan on two properties. Remember, it is short-term financing, typically 6 to 12 months, so you want to make sure that you have an exit strategy as soon as you sell your departing residence in order to pay off that bridge loan and go into whatever your long-term financing is for the remaining house that you now own. But, in the meantime, you have access to deferred payments where you don't have to make any payments on that existing bridge loan while you wait to sell your property. And as soon as that property sold and you actually have those proceeds available to pay off that bridge loan, you're just going to add on however many months you utilize that bridge loan, typically it is an interest-only payment as well. So, those are some of the major pros. Some of the cons of a bridge loan are it is not cheap. I hate to break it to you, but because financing is short-term, just like other loan products we've covered in previous episodes like hard money, the service provider is not going to make any money on this loan because your intention is to pay it off as quickly as possible. So, you can expect to pay anywhere from one to three points on the amount of the total bridge loan financing, in addition to higher interest rates. Now, again, if you're utilizing the deferred financing on an interest-only payment, that's going to help offset some of that all-in cost, but the main reason why you would use a bridge loan is is because it is a immediate vehicle in order for you to secure your upleg or your new property prior to selling your departing residence. So, if you're thinking about making the move and possibly considering a bridge loan, we'd love the opportunity to connect with you and crunch the numbers. You can get in touch with us using our contact information below or drop a question in the comments below, tag it bridge, and I will reply to every single question. Thank you so much again for being a part of the community, and remember to let your income work smarter, not harder. We'll see you on the next one.

metadata.title: Bridge Loans Explained How to Buy Before You Sell and the Free Alternative
metadata.author: Tim Talks Real Estate
metadata.shortDescription:
Thinking about a bridge loan so you can buy your next home before selling your current one? Before you take one out, understand what it really costs — and the free alternative that gets you the same result without the price tag. A mortgage insider since 2007 who originates nothing breaks down exactly how bridge loans work, who they actually fit, and the low-cost move loan officers have the least incentive to mention.

In this video:
- What a bridge loan is and how it "bridges" the gap between buying and selling
- Why bridge loans are one of the most expensive short-term loans in real estate
- The three-payments-at-once trap that catches move-up buyers
- The free alternative: sale contingencies and a pre-set HELOC to buy before you sell
- Who a bridge loan genuinely fits — and who should skip it
- The one question that saves you thousands before you sign

Run the free affordability calculator: https://timtalksrealestate.com/afford
Creative financing breakdown + the free alternative to a bridge loan: https://timtalksrealestate.com/creative-financing

I don't originate loans, so there's nothing being sold to you — just the information.

metadata.title: Don’t Use a Bridge Loan Until You Watch This
metadata.author: RJ Baxter - NEO Home Loans
metadata.shortDescription:
Thinking about a bridge loan to buy your next home in the Denver metro before you sell? This video explains why traditional bridge loans can be expensive and hard to qualify for, and it walks through five alternatives to consider.

I'm RJ Baxter, a mortgage advisor with more than 20 years in the business. I cover a common cap on how much equity a traditional bridge loan will let you access, why qualifying on multiple payments at once can be difficult, and five other approaches: a HELOC, borrowing from a 401(k) or other investments (talk with your plan provider or advisor), a mortgage recast after you sell, a family loan or gift, and "buy before you sell" programs. Every situation is different, so this is a starting point, not a recommendation for one option.

family.
