metadata.title: Private Money Lending Explained: Fast Fix-and-Flip Loans, 75% ARV, and SDIRA Co-Lending with Inve...
metadata.author: Real Estate Explainer
metadata.shortDescription:
How does private money lending work, and why are real estate investors turning to it for faster, more flexible financing? In this episode of the Real Estate Explainer podcast, host Brian Kiczula sits down with Harley Green, founder of InvestAway, to break down private money lending for fix-and-flip investors, rehab projects, and other short-term real estate opportunities.


Harley explains how private money differs from conventional financing and traditional hard money by underwriting deals in-house and using private capital, allowing for quicker decisions and closings for borrowers who may not fit traditional lending criteria. He walks through InvestAway’s typical short-term bridge loans, lending up to 75% of after-repair value (ARV), rehab draw procedures, interest-only structures, and how borrowers are evaluated. Harley also discusses how self-directed IRA investors can participate in first-position real estate loans through co-lending opportunities.


What You’ll Learn in This Episode:

  •  Private Money vs. Traditional Lending: How private money lenders can offer more flexible underwriting and faster closings than conventional financing.
  •  Fix-and-Flip Financing: How short-term bridge loans can help investors purchase, renovate, and reposition real estate.
  •  Lending Up to 75% of ARV: How after-repair value factors into loan sizing and risk management.
  •  Loan Terms and Interest Rates: Why InvestAway’s loans typically run four to nine months, with rates generally ranging from 11.5% to 16%.
  •  Funding the Rehab: How reimbursement-based rehab draws and interest reserves can help investors manage renovation costs and cash flow.
  •  How Deals Are Underwritten: How standard operating procedures, AI tools, third-party valuations, and direct borrower conversations are used to evaluate deals.
  •  When a Project Takes Longer Than Expected: How loan extensions may provide borrowers additional time to complete renovations or sell a property.
  •  Business-Purpose Lending: How private money lending operates across markets including Tennessee, Georgia, Alabama, Missouri, and Indiana.
  •  Self-Directed IRA Co-Lending: How investors may use self-directed retirement accounts to participate in first-position real estate loans.
  •  Selecting Investment Opportunities: How investors can review available loans through a portal, choose individual deals, and participate with a $50,000 minimum investment.
  •  How Investors Get Paid: How principal and returns are typically distributed when the underlying loan is paid off.

Guest Bio:


Harley Green is the founder of InvestAway, a private money lending company focused on helping real estate investors finance short-term acquisitions and renovation projects. InvestAway provides business-purpose bridge financing while also offering qualified investors opportunities to participate in real estate-backed loans, including through self-directed retirement accounts.


Connect with Harley:

  •  Website: InvestAway.co
  •  Email: harley@InvestAway.co (mailto:harley@investaway.com) 
  •  Phone Number: 423-497-0773

Want to connect with today's guest or learn more? Head over to realestateexplainer.com and click the "Get Connected" button on the homepage!

segments.text: Welcome to the Real Estate Explainer
podcast where we talk about anything and
everything real estate. I'm your host
Brian Kicks Unlimited.
>> He sold a house last week in North
Georgia just outside of Chattanooga. He
bought it for 40k, put 60k renovations
in and sold it for 215. Had a six-figure
spread.
>> Welcome back to another episode of the
Real Estate Explainer podcast. I am your
host Brian Kicks Unlimited, a cost
segregation specialist with Cost Seg RX.
Today I have Harley Green with Invest
Away on the podcast and we're going to
be talking about private money lending.
Let's jump right into the episode.
>> I'm Harley Green. I'm the founder of
Invest Away. We do private money
lending. We help borrowers get money
fast and efficiently to buy and renovate
homes quickly. And then we help
investors get secured passive
investments by being the co-lender with
us on these loans. We've been doing it
since 2022. We've funded over $10
million in deals and we have over $6
million in active loans under management
right now. And one of the great things
about this business and this type of
investment for us is that it's given us
a lifestyle where my wife and myself
three young kids are able to be
international nomads full-time. So we've
been around the world. We've been
traveling for over two years. Been to 20
plus different countries and six
continents.
>> That's very cool. And where are you
right now?
>> So we're checking out our beach houses.
We have a couple oceanfront beach houses
in Garden City Beach, South Carolina. So
we're here at the end of the peak season
just kind of doing a refresh on them and
enjoying some time at the beach.
>> Nice. And it's been one of these years.
I'm down in Sarasota, Florida and it is
absolutely beautiful here today. It's
like the humidity dropped off and it's
perfect weather. Can we talk about the
lending aspect? A lot of guys know
traditional financing. Could you talk
about private money and maybe how you're
different?
>> Yeah. So there's kind of three main
categories when it comes to financing in
the real estate world. You've got your
conventional financing, the banks, the
government type backed mortgage options.
Then there's hard money lenders. These
are often like institutionalized, so
they're not necessarily like government,
but they've got big kind of Wall Street
money funding them. They maybe have
underwriting parameters that are very
strict and oftentimes a little bit
faster than those banks, but still
slower than what the third category is
where we fit, which is private money. So
this is where we are the lender. We
become the bank ourselves. We underwrite
the deals ourselves and we make our
funding decisions. And so we can operate
in a space where there's just a gap of
financing options for people who maybe
don't fit typical criteria that the hard
money lenders and traditional banks like
to see. Maybe they don't have a W-2 with
regular income. Maybe they don't have
great credit. We underwrite based on the
asset, and so we're able to take people
that have the skills to do flips, but
maybe don't have the credit that other
financing institutions would fund. And
so that just opens up a wide range of
borrowers who do great work and are
doing, like we said earlier, the single
family homes up to small multi-family.
And it's solving problems on Main
Street. This is the capital that's
needed to renovate homes that are
affordable for like first-time home
buyers and rentals that just is not
happening from other financing
opportunities.
>> My background is mortgages, real estate,
and one of the things that a lot of the
guys would come to me and say, "This is
our own money. We're underwriting and
we're funding our own deals." And I'll
tell you that's just not the case. A lot
of times they'll tell you that, but
you're working with the broker that's
working with a lender, but really
they're working off a line of credit
that they have with another larger
institution. So why they say it's their
own money and they can fund off this
line of credit, that's not the case.
They're still underwriting it off maybe
three sets of underwriting guidelines
that can certainly monkey up the deal,
especially if you're going in and you
found a property that's 50 cents on the
dollar, 75 cents on the dollar retail,
and you're going to go in and make
improvements, and you know you need to
close these things fast, that's where
it's kind of that red flag pops up in my
mind. So, that's the question I kick
back. So, this is your own money that
you're funding with?
>> Yeah, so we underwrite and we fund every
single deal with our own personal
capital. We got into it originally
because my wife had a real estate team
in Tennessee, and she would make
referrals for her buyers to hard money
lenders, and exactly like you said, it's
not really their money. There's
underwriting happening somewhere else,
out of state, and they kick it back cuz
there's one little thing on that
checklist they don't like, and they kill
otherwise good deals. And so, I had just
left a 15-year career as a computer
engineer at that time. I rolled my 401k
into a self-directed IRA, and we started
lending from that. And then, several
years later, we were just looking at
like, what's going well in our
investments, and it was just killing it.
And our borrowers were growing, and they
were referring people, they were wanting
to scale. And so, we actually sold some
of our rental properties that were
underperforming and took that cash to
put into the business. And so,
everything gets funded up front with our
own cash, it's underwritten as if we're
going to hold it for the life of the
loan, and we're totally fine with that.
That's how our family's wealth is being
grown now is in lending. To grow further
though, we opened it up to co-lenders,
and they can come in after we've
originated, and then fractionally
participate as a co-lender alongside of
us.
>> Okay, and then getting back to the loan
itself, so this is a short-term loan,
and it's specifically for real estate
investors that are going in, buying
properties, fixing them, and then
reselling them. Or they're going to hold
on, but they're going to have to take
out their own permanent financing
afterwards. On that short term, what are
the terms of the loan? How long are you
going to hold that loan? And then,
what's the repayment look like? When do
they start making payments? And is it PI
or principal and interest or
interest-only loans until they get
repaid?
>> Now, these are great questions. So, one
of the nice things about being a private
lender is that we can set the terms to
make the deal work. Generally speaking,
our loans are 4 to 9 months on average
across the portfolio, our borrowers exit
the loans in about 6 and 1/2 months. And
so, I'd say about half of them end up
with extensions, but we actually bake
that into the loan documents. We want it
to be something that is clear up front
that our borrowers know is an option if
they need it, so they don't get under
pressure due to time constraints.
Typical like rates and fees, they start
at 11 and 1/2% that goes all the way up
to 16% depending on some of the bells
and whistles that they want and that
goes into the payment structure. We have
the option where if a borrower wants,
they can request a interest reserve on
the loan, so they don't have to make any
payments out of pocket during the life
of the loan. It just gets baked into the
loan up front and comes out of loan as
it's needed like draws for the rehab. Or
they can make interest only payments, so
we don't require principal payments
during the loan. We were active real
estate investors ourselves doing flips
and so we've tried to make a product
that was what we wish we had when we
were doing that. And so it has the
options to make it work for the borrower
and depending on their specific
situation.
>> Yeah, so 11 and 1/2 to 16%. I think a
lot of people that are residential
long-term investors, they're thinking
that is way too high, but we're not
talking about permanent financing. We're
talking about a short-term loan, 4 to 9
months, but even 4 to 9 months, the
thing that folks need to realize is when
they're looking at construction
projects, seems to me like there's
always time delays, overruns and
expenses. So I think that would be my
caution is make sure that when you're
looking at these projects, really
understand the project that you're
getting into. So that's my next question
is what's kind of like the ideal
project, what property should they be
looking at?
>> So our bread and butter across our
portfolio would be homes where the
purchase price is anywhere from 100K to
200K and they're putting in 25 to 100K
of renovations and it's selling for 300.
That's very typical. Now we do some
outlier ones too where people are doing
short-term rentals, they get a property
that needs to be rehabbed and we've had
some of those where the purchase price
is all the way up around 6 to 700,000
and they're putting $200,000 into the
renovation and it's selling for 1 to 1.4
million. So, all those work, it's just
really what we want to focus on is
looking at the borrower and their scope
of work, making sure it makes sense.
Like you said, making sure the scope of
work and the timeline line up with the
options for the loan that they're
requesting. And then also their
experience or their GC's experience. So,
if they're buying a house that's older
than 1950, there's a lot of surprises
that come with houses of that vintage.
And so, we want to make sure that they
or their GC has experience working with
those. And so, that's part of like as a
private lender, we make those phone
calls. When we get an application, we
don't just blindly put it through an
underwriting process. The first thing we
do is we pick up the phone and we have a
conversation about the options they've
selected and the scope of work and the
property to make sure everything makes
sense and they're set up for success.
>> So, a $100,000 to $200,000 purchase
price, it seems to me like in most
markets in the United States, that's
just not a reality. But, I do know that
there are certain markets that you can
still get properties for under $150,000.
And then if you're putting $25,000 into
it, it's a really nice property. But,
even then we have to look at certain
loan-to-value requirements. What type of
LTVs are you looking at?
>> Yeah, so we focus on ARV. And I know a
lot of lenders, they really want to know
the as-is value and the loan-to-value at
any given time. What we have found is
that because these loans are short-term
and we are charging a lot, the borrowers
on day one, they get in and they tear
that place apart and they have their
crews going very quickly. So, any kind
of effort put into like getting an as-is
value and comparing that to your loan
just goes out the window. And so, what
we have found works really well is
saying that we will lend up to 75% of
the ARV. And then we do a
reimbursement-based draw process. So, we
don't just give them a chunk of cash to
do the rehab when the loan closes or do
it based on time. They've got to
demonstrate that they have actually done
work on the house and have paid those
expenses and then they submit for
reimbursement. And so, that way it helps
control and make sure that the money
that we're expending on the asset is
also proportionally adding value to that
asset.
>> Yeah, that absolutely makes sense. When
you're working with the real estate
investor who may be doing 10 of these
projects at once, you want to make sure
that the money that they're drawing on
that loan is actually going into the
house that the loan's tied to. So,
getting the scope of work that's
completed before you do a draw release
absolutely makes sense.
Now, do you assist with permanent
financing if they decide to keep it? Are
you helping with that or are they
strictly fixes and flips?
>> So, we really focus just on that
residential bridge or transition
mortgage. So, getting the purchase and
then renovation or maybe sometimes they
just need fast money to get the
purchase, let it season for a little
bit, and then they'll transition to more
permanent financing. We have tried doing
like other brokering the DSR type loans
and stuff like that. The thing that I
have just found over and over is that my
word and our speed and our service and
the certainty that we give our borrowers
is what they're paying for. And when I'm
brokering a loan and it's not my money,
it's somebody else, and I don't control
the yeses or the nos or the asks, it
creates problems. And so, I've just said
no. We can refer them to other brokers
or other lenders. They can deal with
that. It is not the business that we
want to be in.
>> I agree. So, what we're talking about,
too, which I think is super important,
is certainty. So, knowing that once you
get a deal that financially makes sense,
it can be underwritten, you've got the
correct loan-to-value in place or
after-repaired value in place,
and a team, you can execute. So, you're
able to close on the deal and move
forward. So, I think that is one thing
that private money lenders absolutely
crush it at compared to retail brokers.
And then, as far as the underwriting
requirements go, how do you vet the deal
since you are underwriting these files?
>> I'd like to thank today's sponsor, Cost
Seg RX, a cost segregation company. If
you're interested in getting a cost
segregation study, or if you'd like a
free estimate of benefit, log on to
realestateexplainer.com
and click the cost segregation link at
the top of the page.
>> Yeah, so my background's engineering. We
use a lot of SOPs and a lot of AI to
automate as much as possible. So, we go
through and we actually have AI agents
can do things like call whether it's in
a rural zone or not, whether it's in a
flood zone or not, analyze all the
photos they submit to see the condition.
We use a third-party evaluation service
that asks for some of the information
that we assess to get the ARV. And so,
the human part comes in really on that
phone call after we've done all this
automated underwriting and we have all
the data, then we have a phone call to
make sure the scope of work makes sense
based on the current condition and the
timeline they have selected. And then,
we found that by having that 75% margin
against the ARV across our portfolio and
our history, we've never had to do a
foreclosure. The worst that's happened
to happen is just do a couple of
extensions to give someone more time. I
think that's in a large part because we
just make sure that the house value
after repair and of course that ARV is
coming looking backwards and we're
focusing on markets that are growth
markets and they're adding value. So, we
get some help there and between that and
having these borrowers that know that,
hey, if they do well by us, we really
can open the floodgate for them. We do
things like after three deals, they can
have 0% down, so they've got infinite
returns. We've had really good success
with great repeat borrowers and never
had to do a foreclosure.
>> That's awesome. And then, as far as the
markets that you're lending in, are you
tied to a couple of markets or you
lending all across the United States?
>> So, it's an interesting like function.
So, as a private lender, we do business
purpose loans only. So, we're not going
to help people buy their primary
residence. In fact, they can never have
even owned it in their personal name
before or we will not lend on it. It's
got to be pure like arms length
transaction going into a business entity
for business purposes, either flipped or
turning into a rental. And so, that kind
of controls some of the states that
we're allowed to lend in because we do
not have a normal residential mortgage
broker license. And so, that kind of
eliminates some states right there. Then
the other things we focus on is again,
like I said, we want to be in high
growth markets. So we kind of have a
preference right now of like Tennessee,
Georgia, Alabama, Missouri. And we have
a lot of loans in certain markets in
Indiana. And that's because that's where
people are moving. There's a lot of
those homes that are in that price
point. In fact, we just funded a few
this last week. They're like 20, 30,000
dollar purchases and they cash flow
right away for these people getting like
a seller financing deal. And so the
deals are out there and we focus on
those types of markets that are friendly
for lenders and licensing requirements.
>> Okay. Yeah, that absolutely makes sense.
And when I'm doing cost segregation
studies across the United States, I get
a lot of clients that say, "Is it worth
it for me to do a cost segregation study
on this property?" And sometimes it'll
be in markets where the basis is only
and I'll say, "We need to take a look."
And the answer is most likely yes, it
does make sense. But I've gotten into
the conversations where the clients
don't own one property, they own a
portfolio and every year they're buying
another portfolio. So I think it's
probably that same thing with you as you
work with a client, maybe they'll do one
or two properties, three properties and
it turns out that they're really turning
20, 100 properties a year. Maybe they're
keeping some of them in their own
portfolio. So very cool stuff. To switch
gears a little bit, you hit on it at the
very beginning of the call and it was a
self-directed IRA. I think this is so
cool. Not only is it something that you
offer, but it's something that you
personally did to get the business
started. So you have personal experience
because when you're looking at doing a
self-directed IRA, it's your retirement
account. So there's definitely some
concern about investing in something
that's a little bit unknown. So if you
could tell us how that works a little
bit.
>> Yeah, so we first started the
self-directed IRA to jump in and save
these deals that we knew were good
investments. And so for us it was like
worst case if the borrower doesn't pay,
we foreclose, we take over the property,
and we finish the flip and likely make
more money. Thankfully, it never had to
happen. We've never had to foreclose,
like I said, and it's been a great
investment for the SD IRA. I recommend
it for anyone else who's thinking about
doing private lending is consider if you
have the ability to have a self-directed
IRA because it's a tax-advantaged
investment vehicle. And with private
lending, unlike direct real estate
ownership, there's not tax benefits.
You're just getting that interest
income. There's no depreciation. So,
having it in a tax-advantaged vehicle
makes a lot of sense. And also, it's one
of the things that can be very passive
and help really keep the line clear of
like the SD IRA and IRS regulations
about like adding value to like your own
retirement account. When people get into
some potential gray areas if they're
like buying a rental property in their
SD IRA, and then they're going out and
like doing the work on it and adding the
value themselves, well, maybe nobody's
going to check that, but it could create
potential conflicts. And so, going and
being private lender where you're just
lending the money, you're collecting
interest, and partnering with a company
like ours, it makes it all very clean
and very easy.
>> So, what the self-directed IRA is what
we're talking about where you're making
investment decisions on your own. And
we're also talking about the
self-dealing. So, you can't take the
money,
buy a property, flip it, take the
proceeds, put it in your pocket because
then you'd be paying yourself. All of
the proceeds need to go back into the
IRA. You can't even manage it. You can't
purchase a property in an IRA and then
self-management. Everything has to go
back into that self-directed IRA. And
how did you avoid that? How were you
able to do that in your own business?
>> Yeah, so for the lending, the way we
worked around that is we co-originate.

videos.full_text: Welcome to the Real Estate Explainer podcast where we talk about anything and everything real estate. I'm your host Brian Kicks Unlimited. >> He sold a house last week in North Georgia just outside of Chattanooga. He bought it for 40k, put 60k renovations in and sold it for 215. Had a six-figure spread. >> Welcome back to another episode of the Real Estate Explainer podcast. I am your host Brian Kicks Unlimited, a cost segregation specialist with Cost Seg RX. Today I have Harley Green with Invest Away on the podcast and we're going to be talking about private money lending. Let's jump right into the episode. >> I'm Harley Green. I'm the founder of Invest Away. We do private money lending. We help borrowers get money fast and efficiently to buy and renovate homes quickly. And then we help investors get secured passive investments by being the co-lender with us on these loans. We've been doing it since 2022. We've funded over $10 million in deals and we have over $6 million in active loans under management right now. And one of the great things about this business and this type of investment for us is that it's given us a lifestyle where my wife and myself three young kids are able to be international nomads full-time. So we've been around the world. We've been traveling for over two years. Been to 20 plus different countries and six continents. >> That's very cool. And where are you right now? >> So we're checking out our beach houses. We have a couple oceanfront beach houses in Garden City Beach, South Carolina. So we're here at the end of the peak season just kind of doing a refresh on them and enjoying some time at the beach. >> Nice. And it's been one of these years. I'm down in Sarasota, Florida and it is absolutely beautiful here today. It's like the humidity dropped off and it's perfect weather. Can we talk about the lending aspect? A lot of guys know traditional financing. Could you talk about private money and maybe how you're different? >> Yeah. So there's kind of three main categories when it comes to financing in the real estate world. You've got your conventional financing, the banks, the government type backed mortgage options. Then there's hard money lenders. These are often like institutionalized, so they're not necessarily like government, but they've got big kind of Wall Street money funding them. They maybe have underwriting parameters that are very strict and oftentimes a little bit faster than those banks, but still slower than what the third category is where we fit, which is private money. So this is where we are the lender. We become the bank ourselves. We underwrite the deals ourselves and we make our funding decisions. And so we can operate in a space where there's just a gap of financing options for people who maybe don't fit typical criteria that the hard money lenders and traditional banks like to see. Maybe they don't have a W-2 with regular income. Maybe they don't have great credit. We underwrite based on the asset, and so we're able to take people that have the skills to do flips, but maybe don't have the credit that other financing institutions would fund. And so that just opens up a wide range of borrowers who do great work and are doing, like we said earlier, the single family homes up to small multi-family. And it's solving problems on Main Street. This is the capital that's needed to renovate homes that are affordable for like first-time home buyers and rentals that just is not happening from other financing opportunities. >> My background is mortgages, real estate, and one of the things that a lot of the guys would come to me and say, "This is our own money. We're underwriting and we're funding our own deals." And I'll tell you that's just not the case. A lot of times they'll tell you that, but you're working with the broker that's working with a lender, but really they're working off a line of credit that they have with another larger institution. So why they say it's their own money and they can fund off this line of credit, that's not the case. They're still underwriting it off maybe three sets of underwriting guidelines that can certainly monkey up the deal, especially if you're going in and you found a property that's 50 cents on the dollar, 75 cents on the dollar retail, and you're going to go in and make improvements, and you know you need to close these things fast, that's where it's kind of that red flag pops up in my mind. So, that's the question I kick back. So, this is your own money that you're funding with? >> Yeah, so we underwrite and we fund every single deal with our own personal capital. We got into it originally because my wife had a real estate team in Tennessee, and she would make referrals for her buyers to hard money lenders, and exactly like you said, it's not really their money. There's underwriting happening somewhere else, out of state, and they kick it back cuz there's one little thing on that checklist they don't like, and they kill otherwise good deals. And so, I had just left a 15-year career as a computer engineer at that time. I rolled my 401k into a self-directed IRA, and we started lending from that. And then, several years later, we were just looking at like, what's going well in our investments, and it was just killing it. And our borrowers were growing, and they were referring people, they were wanting to scale. And so, we actually sold some of our rental properties that were underperforming and took that cash to put into the business. And so, everything gets funded up front with our own cash, it's underwritten as if we're going to hold it for the life of the loan, and we're totally fine with that. That's how our family's wealth is being grown now is in lending. So, one of the nice things about being a private lender is that we can set the terms to make the deal work. Generally speaking, our loans are 4 to 9 months on average across the portfolio, our borrowers exit the loans in about 6 and 1/2 months. And so, I'd say about half of them end up with extensions, but we actually bake that into the loan documents. We want it to be something that is clear up front that our borrowers know is an option if they need it, so they don't get under pressure due to time constraints. metadata.title: What is a bridge loan - How do bridge loans work?
metadata.author: Jeb Smith
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you looking to purchase a home before selling your current home but need the cash from that home for a down payment?  Have you considering a bridge loan?  What is a bridge loan?  How does a bridge loan work?  A bridge loan is a short term loan that can help you buy a new home before you sell your current one by using the equity from your existing home.  In this video, I talk about bridge loan financing in more detail and help you understand how they work and how it could benefit you in making a non-contingent offer to purchase a new home.

#RealEstate #RealEstateMarket #HousingMarket

New videos every week – Subscribe here: https://goo.gl/NZB1S6

 What is a Bridge Loan - Bridge loans are a short term loan that allow you to borrow the equity from your current home to buy another home without selling that home first.  

How do you qualify for a bridge loan - It’s more or less the same as qualifying for a traditional loan but lenders are primarily looking for equity on your current residence so that the bridge loan makes sense.  I’ve seen a lot of lenders allow higher debt to income ratios on bridge loans when there is a significant amount of equity.  Bridge loans roll the mortgages of two houses together, giving the buyer flexibility as they wait for their old house to sell. However, in most cases, lenders only offer real estate bridge loans worth 80% of the combined value of the two properties At the end of the day you more or less have to show that you have the ability to pay for both mortgages.

Are bridge loans a good idea - each person’s scenario is different so there can be a blanket answer on this but in theory bridge loans are a good idea if you have equity and want to make an offer on a new house without selling your existing home first or without making a non-contingent offer.  Most bridge loan lenders will allow you to defer the mortgage payment for a period of time (usually around 6 months up to a year) until your home sells.  At which point it sells, you will be required to pay that deferred interest.  

The downside usually comes if your home doesn’t sell and you start to feel the pressure of having the bridge loan and the lender starts making you make both mortgage payments.  That could put you in a situation where you have to sell your home for less money than you intiially wanted just to get out of the situation.  

Are bridge loans expensive - bridge loans generally have interest rates and fees higher than traditional loans and you will likely have to refinance once your homes sells into a new mortgage getting rid of the bridge loan so you will end up paying more fees doing a bridge loan but it also allows you to be in a better position when you purchase so you have to weigh both scenarios and figure out what works best for your situation.

If you are considering selling your home and have questions about bridge loans or bridge loan financing, please comment below or contact me directly.

metadata.title: What is Commercial Bridge Financing and Loan Exit Plans Explained
metadata.author: MKK Capital Commercial Hard Money Lenders
metadata.shortDescription:
Commercial Bridge Financing and Loan Exit Plans
Commercial bridge financing is a short-term capital solution used in commercial real estate when a property is in transition and cannot yet qualify for traditional long-term financing. Investors and developers use bridge loans to acquire, improve, stabilize, or reposition a property while working toward a defined financial destination. The purpose of bridge financing is speed, flexibility, and the ability to fund a project based on its future potential rather than its current condition.

Bridge loans typically run between six and thirty-six months. They are interest-only, asset-focused, and built around the business plan for the property. Lenders evaluate the value of the real estate, the strength of the sponsor, the timeline for improvements, and the projected net operating income once the plan is complete. Because the loan is short-term, rates are higher than permanent financing, but the tradeoff is fast approval and the ability to close quickly on opportunities that traditional lenders cannot support.

Investors use bridge financing for several reasons. Some need to acquire a property before it hits the market. Others need capital to renovate units, improve occupancy, complete construction, or refinance maturing debt. Bridge financing is also used when a property’s financials are not yet strong enough for agency or bank underwriting. In all cases, the bridge loan acts as a temporary solution that allows the investor to move forward without waiting for the property to stabilize.

A bridge loan is only successful when it has a clear and realistic exit plan. The exit plan is the strategy for paying off the bridge loan once the transition period is complete. Lenders require this plan at the start of the loan because it determines the feasibility of the project and the risk level of the transaction.

The most common exit is refinancing into permanent debt. Once renovations are complete, occupancy increases, and net operating income improves, the property can qualify for long-term financing such as agency loans, CMBS, bank loans, or life-company financing. This exit lowers the interest rate, extends the amortization period, and allows the investor to hold the property for cash flow.

Another common exit is selling the property. Many value-add investors use bridge financing to acquire, improve, and reposition an asset, then sell it at a higher valuation. The sale proceeds pay off the bridge loan and generate profit for the investor.

Owner-operators may exit into SBA financing once their business performance meets the required benchmarks. SBA 504 and SBA 7(a) loans offer long-term stability for companies that occupy their own commercial real estate.

In rare cases, strong cash flow created during the transition period can repay the bridge loan directly. This is less common but possible when the business plan significantly increases revenue.

A well-defined exit plan is the foundation of any successful bridge loan. Without it, the project carries unnecessary risk and may not qualify for funding. With it, bridge financing becomes a powerful tool that allows investors to move quickly, unlock value, and position their properties for long-term success. For more and bridge loan calculator information  visit https://calhardmoneylenders.com/commercial-bridge-loans/

segments.text: Commercial bridge loans are built for
speed in solving the timing problems
that slow down real estate deals.
While they are more flexible than bank
loans, lenders still follow a specific
pattern for qualification.
The first thing a lender looks at isn't
you, it's the property itself.
They are looking for strong collateral
and a value that reflects the current
market reality.
Because these are asset-driven loans,
the property carries the most weight in
the decision.
If the numbers make sense and there is
enough equity, you are already halfway
to an approval.
Next, the focus shifts to your
experience and how it aligns with the
project.
You don't need a 30-year history, but
you do need a track record that matches
the asset type.
If you are renovating a multi-family
complex, the lender wants to see that
you have done it before.
Proven experience reduces the lender's
risk, which usually leads to better
pricing for you.
Then comes financial strength, which is
more about responsibility than a perfect
credit score.
Lenders check your liquidity and
reserves to ensure you can handle
unexpected renovation costs.
Having cash on hand and a clear
explanation for any past credit issues
goes a long way.
The fourth factor is your business plan,
specifically how you intend to [music]
pay the loan back.
A bridge loan is temporary, so a
believable exit strategy is
non-negotiable.
Will you refinance into a long-term
conventional loan once the property is
stabilized?
Or is the plan to improve the asset's
value and sell it for a profit?
A realistic plan shows the lender that
this is a true bridge, not a long-term
risk.
Finally, timing and communication
determine who gets to the closing table
first.
Bridge loans move fast, and lenders
expect borrowers to keep up with that
pace.

And in those situations, we're looking at it just like a bank will. You know, we're going to look at their secondary sources of income and re and ability to repay. If it's a startup business, we need to make sure that they have the ability to repay even if that startup fails. We're going to look at the underlying real estate, make sure it's valuable enough if they had to close that business and and lease it up or or sell as well and look at their secondary sources of income. So, it's very dependent on the situation, what we require, very minimum, it's very streamlined stuff. So, >> wow, that's great. What risk should a multifamily investor consider when they're coming to you asking for either a bridge loan or private money? The >> risk they should consider in the property or >> Yeah. Yeah. Often I find that people maybe haven't really thought I I just got a call last week. Some people had bought some land in West Eugene. They were going to build six town houses for middle housing density. They went to a commercial lender. They got the first two built. In my opinion, they're overpriced by at least 50,000. Could be even more. I don't sell residential, but I could just look at it and look at Zillow and some quick facts and I'm like, "Oo, you're at least 50 over the market." They've been on the market 90 days. They have to sell these two in order to get the commercial lender to give them more money to build the other four. They're trying to help their son become a developer. So, it's mom and dad and an adult son. And I don't think they really factored in the risk of what happens if these two properties don't sell. And they called me and said, "Hey, give us a value." And I'm like, "Oh, this is really tough because a contractor is not going to want to step in the middle without a huge discount. You're probably not going to want to give up that discount." So from a risk aspect when you're underwriting things and trying to advise people, what pitfalls or risks should they consider that maybe they haven't thought of yet, but you you see it through your underwriting lens. >> Yeah. I'll start off by saying, you know, I caution people away from deals more often than I actually close them [laughter] because they'll they'll come to me with those rosecolored glasses. Maybe they the very first thing that I I look at in their underwriting is their as complete or after repair value estimate. Is that realistic? Are their costs realistic? And if they seem a little off to me upfront, are these individuals maybe getting a bit too emotional? Maybe they need to step back. I mean, real estate investing should not be purely, it can be, but it shouldn't be if you're doing it as an investor, a passion project. >> So, when you know, I see a project like you just described with a a family, they're trying to get into development, they get excited or I look at a lot of deals from architects. I love architects and designers. First thing they love to do is they design cool buildings. And I love cool buildings, but are they cost-effective to build? Not always. And do they actually know where their costs are or where the end value is? That end value oftent times with an architect is going to be slightly inflated because they think their building is the most beautiful and it's going to be the top of the market. And you got to be realistic. So from a risk standpoint, you got to be able to step back as an investor and be objective, not get emotional. Look at the facts, look at the numbers, not have those rosecolored glasses on, and really get realistic and conservative with your estimates. If you hit a home run like you hope to, that's great, but you've got to go in with that. I don't want to say worst case scenario can always go really really bad, but a bad case scenario in mind. >> You say that all the time, Renee. [laughter] >> I know. I I do. I just I've seen so many train wrecks. >> That's your mantra is like >> like take the emotions out, step back, look at the deal with the numbers. And I think it is hard cuz we do have like you were saying architects and then it's like they want to design this beautiful building. I I actually think it's so funny. I was learning about like design build versus architects and builders separately. I mean, I don't know a lot about commercial estate other than what we've talked about on this show, but I think it is so funny to me that the industry as a whole was always separate. It was like designers and builders and engineers and everything is separate. But then we're sort of now seeing the rise in these design build companies where they do all of it like start to finish all under one house and you can get your budget like a little bit more aligned from the start. It's so funny to me that it wasn't the industry wasn't always that way that it's only now like starting to become a thing. >> Yeah. the companies that can, you know, at the same time plan from a cost perspective and a functionality perspective and make that synergy, they're successful. The ones where you get this design in your head that's this beautiful, amazing building, well, you got to be able to build it. It has to pencil and make sense. I have a neighbor that's an architect and he builds commercial designs commercial stuff and he's freaking amazing at what he does. But he's told me that it was like playing with Legos and Tinker Toys as a kid that gave him those ideas and that's still how he envisions what he does and he's really good at what he does. But sometimes I see his stuff and I'm like, "Oh, I would not want the bill for that for building it." You know, cuz like you're saying, it doesn't always pencil. It may be beautiful, but you know, and interestingly, like we've also noticed, I don't know if you see this, Zach, but leads and some of those other really important factors, those seem to have tapered off because to build to a lead certification, it's so expensive in Eugene that a lot of people are like, I can't afford that. I'm curious, Zach, if you were giving advice to either your family member or a close loved one, what would you tell them and insist on they make sure are in a loan terms or a loan structure to protect themselves? What would be something important for them to be aware of? >> Yeah, in particular in my industry niche and bridge lending, bridge lenders, hard money lenders, it's really the wild west. There are a lot of different terms that can be snuck in there in your term sheet. One important one is Dutch interest. So essentially, like I said before, some lenders, they'll match an individual or group of investors to a loan. Oftent times those private lenders have to fund 100% of their loan into escrow and then that money is gradually dispersed to the borrower if it's a construction loan. But investors do interest on that entire loan balance from day one, whether the borrower's drawn in it or not. So with groundup construction, you could have a $1.5 million construction loan that's getting charged interest on $1.5 million from day one, but yet you only have 250,000 of it outstanding. So we don't charge Dutch interest because of of our fund model. That's one thing that's important to consider that people don't realize on the private money side and a lot of the institutional I I'll call that institutional lenders more of the regional or national bridge lenders they don't have the local expertise number one so they're very difficult to work with in a state like Oregon that has a lot of moving parts and then number two they oftent times will package in just a ton of junk fees. They have that beautiful low interest rate because they got that hedge fund money somewhere and they got that low origination fee that they market, but then on top of the origination fee, you got a fee for every email they send you or every draw request if you're doing a construction loan. So the junk fees and the hidden fees are can get kind of crazy from hard money lenders and that's why we just try and streamline everything for people and operate with transparency. >> Oh, that's really cool. metadata.title: Transactional Funding - Proof of Funds Letters
metadata.author: Foreclosure University
metadata.shortDescription:
Transactional Funding - http://www.foreclosureuniversity.com/studycenter/freereports/transactional_funding.php

Transactional funding is a process where money is used on a short term basis to facilitate a transaction between a seller and buyer.  It's becoming increasingly popular among real estate investors because of how easy it is to use and the many benefits that come with it.

These funds can be used in any of the 50 states in the U.S.  We are experienced real estate professionals so it doesn't matter where you where.  The important thing to understand it that it's a back to back closing.  

A lot of people get transactional funding mixed up with long term funding like a hard money loan.  Whenever you have an end buyer in place, this is where our funding shines.  Short sale, REO's, Bulk REO's, wholesale deals, anything that doesn't involve holding.  Rehabbing is a good example of what we DO NOT fund.

You only have the funds long enough to facilitate the 2 transactions that happen back to back.  We understand that in some cases certain banks require hold periods.  No problem.  We can fund up to 45 days with our extended transactional funding.

This is technically not a loan that you might be accustomed to which is why we don't require any credit checks or employment verification.  All we require is that you have your end buyer in place, both purchase and sale agreements, funding request form and escrow receipt.  We'll take care of the rest.

We look forward to helping you fund your deals and becoming your long term transactional funding partner.


http://www.foreclosureuniversity.com/studycenter/freereports/transactional_funding.php

metadata.title: Earnest Money in Greenwich, CT with Charles Nedder
metadata.author: Charles Nedder | Greenwich CT Real Estate
metadata.shortDescription:
Buying in Greenwich? Don't Lose Your Deposit! 

Most buyers in Greenwich, Connecticut, have no idea where their earnest money actually goes. They assume it goes to the seller—it doesn’t. If the deal falls apart, getting that money back isn't always a guarantee.

In this video, Charles Nedder pulls back the curtain on the Greenwich real estate market to show you exactly how the escrow process works, who controls your cash, and the one thing that protects you more than anything else.

What You’ll Learn:

The 10% Rule: Why Greenwich timelines feel "fast" compared to other markets.

The Attorney Advantage: Why Greenwich, CT doesn't use title companies for escrow.

Contingency Protection: How to ensure your deposit is returned if the deal fails.

Dispute Deadlocks: What happens when the buyer and seller don't agree to release funds?

Chapter Timestamps (Quick Access)

00:00:00 – The Deposit Myth: Where your money really goes.

00:00:54 – Who holds the check? (Buyer vs. Seller Attorneys).

00:01:54 – The 10% Custom: Why you need to be ready to wire funds fast.

00:02:34 – Termination Truths: Can you actually get your money back?

00:03:16 – The Escrow Trap: When funds get stuck for months.

00:03:49 – Your Best Defense: The power of the written contract.

00:05:01 – Closing Thoughts & How to work with Charles.

Frequently Asked Questions: Earnest Money in Greenwich, CT

1. Where is my earnest money held during the transaction?
In Greenwich, CT, your deposit does not go to the seller or a real estate brokerage. It is initially wired to your buyer’s attorney, who then forwards it to the seller’s attorney. The funds are held in the seller’s attorney’s escrow account until the closing.

2. How much is the standard earnest money deposit in Greenwich?
Local custom in the Greenwich market is typically 10% of the purchase price. This is usually due at the time the formal contract is signed, which often happens within 5 days of your offer being accepted.

3. Is my deposit refundable if I change my mind?
Your deposit is protected by contingencies written into your contract (such as home inspection or mortgage financing). If you terminate the contract within these contingency periods for a valid reason, your deposit is generally returned. However, if these periods have expired, your deposit may be at risk.

4. What happens if there is a dispute over the deposit?
If a deal falls apart and there is a disagreement about who gets the money, both the buyer’s and seller’s attorneys must agree on the release of funds. If they cannot reach an agreement, the money stays in escrow until a court makes a decision, which can take months or longer.

5. When is the deal officially "secure"?
In Connecticut, a deal is not legally binding or secure until both parties have signed the formal contract and the deposit has been delivered. Until both steps are complete, either the buyer or the seller can walk away from the deal.

Connect With Charles Nedder
Navigating the Greenwich, CT real estate landscape requires local expertise and a proactive strategy. If you're looking to buy or sell, let’s talk!

Direct: 203-524-4303
Email: sales@cnedder.com

Follow for more Greenwich Market Updates!

And you will understand the one thing that protects you more than anything else in this process. So, let us start with where the money actually goes. In Connecticut, your earnest money deposit does not go to the seller. It does not go to the listing agent. It does not sit in a real estate brokerage account. Your deposit goes to your attorney, the buyer's attorney. Your attorney then [music] sends the deposit along with the buyer signed contract to the seller's attorney. From there, the money sits in the seller's [music] attorney's escrow account untouched until the deal either closes or falls apart. This is different from a lot of other states where the listing brokerage or a title company [music] holds the deposit. Here in Greenwich, Connecticut, the process runs through the attorneys on both sides. That is an important distinction because it means licensed professionals representing [music] each party are the ones handling your money from start to finish. Now, here is where it gets practical. In Greenwich, once your offer [music] is accepted, both attorneys get to work negotiating the contract terms. That process can move [music] quickly. Your attorney handles the release. But, here is what most buyers do not expect. If the contingency periods have expired and you decide to walk away, [music] it is not as simple as asking for your money back. In Connecticut, both the buyer's attorney and the seller's attorney must agree to release the funds. >> [music] >> If one side disputes the release, that deposit stays in escrow. This is exactly why your attorney reviews every deadline [music] and every contingency in the contract before you sign. Those dates are not suggestions. metadata.title: What Is an Earnest Money Deposit? (And How to Protect It)
metadata.author: Beyond the Address
metadata.shortDescription:
Did you know you could lose thousands of dollars if you don't understand how an earnest money deposit works? Kim Haber of Beyond Realty breaks down what earnest money (EMD) is, how much it typically is, where it goes, how buyers can lose it, and how to protect your deposit.

In this video, we cover:

What an earnest money deposit (a "good faith deposit") is.

A real example: 3% of a $650,000 offer equals $19,500.

Where the money is held and how it's applied at closing.

How buyers can forfeit their deposit, and how contingencies protect it.

The three key contingencies: financing, home inspection, and appraisal.

How to send your deposit safely (wire transfer vs. cashier's check).

Earnest money explained: 

So what is an earnest money deposit (EMD) anyway?  The earnest money deposit meaning is simply a deposit of good faith in a real estate transaction into the escrow account by the buyer to the seller to show sincerity and intent to purchase their house.  

You may wondering what is the earnest money deposit amount, right?  Well the earnest money amount is actually based upon an earnest money deposit percentage usually between 1%- 3% of the list price of the home.  Example = $400,000 list price * 2% = $8,000 earnest money.  

Why should you know how protect earnest money?  That's simple... This is YOUR hard earned money you're putting up for your new place to call home.  If something goes awry with the home inspections, your buyer due diligence, or the home appraisal shouldn't you be able to get a earnest money refund?  Of course!

In this video you'll learn you how to protect earnest money deposit, by:

2.  Get everything in writing

metadata.title: How can buyers protect their earnest money deposit in Florida?
metadata.author: Larry Mastropieri
metadata.shortDescription:
While buyers aim to close after a smooth inspection, the legal priority is keeping the escrow safe in case the deal must be canceled—most commonly because inspections reveal problems or financing falls through.

The single best protection is strict compliance with the contract’s timelines and conditions. If the inspection period is ten days and talks over repairs or credits stall, the buyer must cancel within that window—by day nine or ten at the latest—to preserve the deposit. Missing the deadline can jeopardize the money, so calendar control is everything.

Larry Mastropieri explains how a well-run buyer’s agent function acts as the second line of defense after the buyer’s own diligence. His team runs 8 a.m. operations check-ins every day and reads off every active contract’s critical dates from a shared calendar, marking which items are on track, at risk, or in trouble. That discipline helps them proactively address issues before a deadline passes. Because every contract is unique, they track not just the inspection/due-diligence period but also the loan-commitment deadline, any appraisal timing, and other contingencies like a sale-of-home clause. Each of these can independently determine whether the buyer keeps or forfeits the escrow.

A key operational habit: confirm feasibility with all third parties before accepting aggressive timelines. If a seller wants a 14-day loan commitment, Larry immediately loops in the lender and buyer to confirm documents, appraisal scheduling, and underwriting capacity. If it’s a lender they don’t usually work with, Larry seeks repeated, explicit assurances so there’s no ambiguity later. The north star throughout is simple—hit every contractual milestone or formally cancel within the contingency period if the deal’s not trending right—so the escrow deposit stays protected.

metadata.title: Don't Lose Your Deposit! Protect Your Earnest Money When Buying a Home
metadata.author: James Brinkman
metadata.shortDescription:
Don't Lose Your Deposit! How to Really Protect Your Earnest Money When Buying a Home
How Your Earnest Money Deposit Could Disappear Overnight is something every homebuyer needs to understand—especially in a competitive housing market. Your earnest money deposit (EMD) isn’t just a formality; it’s serious money at risk if things go wrong. In this video, James Brinkman, aka Brink, breaks down the basics of how an earnest money deposit works, what can cause you to lose it, and most importantly, how to protect it with contingencies like financing, inspection, and appraisal clauses. Whether you're buying your first home or your fifth, understanding the rules around EMD can save you thousands of dollars. Learn how escrow works, the forms of payment you’ll need, and the crucial role your real estate agent plays in keeping your deposit safe. Don’t let a contract slip-up cost you big—watch now and be prepared to buy smart!

3 Key Takeaways
Earnest money is not a guarantee—you can lose it.
If you back out without a valid contractual reason, that money may legally belong to the seller.

Contingencies are your safety net.
Properly negotiated contingencies (financing, inspection, appraisal) protect your deposit if something goes sideways.

Don’t wing it—work with professionals.
An experienced agent and escrow officer will walk you through your best payment options and ensure your deposit is handled securely.

Step-by-Step: How to Protect Your Earnest Money Deposit

Understand What EMD Is: It’s a good faith deposit, usually around 1–3% of the home’s price, showing the seller you’re serious.

Know When to Submit It: You send this in when your offer is accepted—typically within 1–3 business days.

Use the Right Form of Payment: Only wire transfers or cashier’s checks are accepted. Forget cash, debit, or credit.

Negotiate Contingencies: Work with your agent to ensure financing, inspection, and appraisal contingencies are in place.

Stick to Your Contract Timeline: If you miss deadlines or fail to act in good faith, you risk losing the deposit.

Back Out Only Within Contingency Windows: These give you a legal and financial “exit ramp” if needed.

FAQ
1. How much should I put down as earnest money?
Typically 1–3% of the purchase price. In competitive markets, more may help your offer stand out.

2. Can I lose my earnest money?
Yes—if you back out of the deal without a valid contractual reason.

3. Who holds my earnest money?
Usually a title company or escrow officer—never the buyer or seller directly.

4. Is earnest money refundable?
Only if you exit the contract within agreed-upon contingencies or due to seller breach.

5. What happens to the earnest money at closing?
It’s applied toward your down payment or closing costs.

One of the biggest fears buyers have is losing their earnest money deposit 😰

Here’s the good news 👇

Earnest money, also called the initial deposit, is the money you put down after your offer is accepted 📝 It goes into an escrow account to be held until close. It’s usually about 1–3% of the purchase price and shows the seller you’re serious 🤝

But it’s not automatically at risk.

That’s because of contingencies 🛡️

Contingencies are built-in protections that give buyers a way out if something isn’t right. If a contingency isn’t met, or you change your mind before removing all contingencies, you can cancel the contract and keep your earnest money.

Common contingencies include:
• loan approval 💰
• appraisal coming in at value 📊
• inspections and investigations 🔍

In short, your earnest money stays protected until contingencies are removed 🔒

This is why having the right buyer’s agent matters 👥
We make sure everything checks out before moving forward.

Why promissory notes with a deed of trust beat land contracts for vacant land sales — and how the choice affects your land note's resale value. Land note buyers won't purchase land contracts.

segments.text: Welcome to module six. This is one of
the most important modules in this
entire course. The decision you make
here whether to use a land contract or a
promisory note with a deed of trust or
mortgage will determine whether you can
easily sell your notes, protect yourself
legally and avoid massive headaches down
the road. Let me be very clear from the
start. Always use a promisory note with
a deed of trust or mortgage. Don't use
land contracts. Let me quickly explain
but what we're talking about. A land
contract, also called a contract for
deed, is an agreement where the seller
retains legal title of the property
until the buyer pays off the entire
purchase price. The buyer gets equitable
title and the right to possess the
property, but the seller remains the
legal owner on the deed until the
contract is fully paid. A promisory note
with a deed of trust or mortgage works
differently. The property immediately
deeds to the buyer at closing. The buyer
becomes the legal owner, but the seller
holds a lean on the property through the
deed of trust or mortgage, which secures
the promisory note. If the buyer doesn't
pay, the seller can foreclose. Now, let
me explain why the second option is
dramatically better. There are about 10
reasons that I don't like land
contracts. Let me walk through the major
ones.
First, you own the property. With a land
contract, you remain the legal owner of
the property until it's paid off. This
means you're liable for anything that
happens on that property. If someone
gets hurt on the property, you could be
sued. You will need to maintain
liability insurance on a property you
don't control. This is a terrible
position to be in. Second, they're much
harder to sell to note buyers. When you
try to sell a land contract to a note
buyer like me, it's much more
complicated. I not only have to buy the
contract from you, I also have to get
the property deed to me, which involves
additional paperwork, transfer taxes,
and the loss of coverage for the owner's
title policy.
Many note buyers won't touch land
contracts at all because of these
complications.
Third, transfer tax issues when the loan
is paid off.
When the buyer finally pays off a land
contract, you have to deed the property
to them. In many states, this triggers
transfer taxes all over again. So, the
buyer ends up paying transfer taxes
twice. Once when you originally sold it
and again when they finished paying and
you deed it to them. This is a totally
unnecessary expense.
Fourth, complicated and varying state
laws. Every state handles land contracts
differently and some states don't even
have laws at all for them. Some states
treat them more like mortgages. Others
treat them like leases. The legal
requirements and processes vary
dramatically.
What works in one state may not work in
another and this can actually work
against you as an investor. Fifth,
there's a dangerous misconception.
Many people think that if the buyer
stops paying on a land contract, you
just cancel the contract and resell the
property to someone else. This sounds
simple, but it's completely wrong in
most states. You typically have to go
through a formal legal process to cancel
the contract, and in many states, that
process looks a lot like foreclosure
anyway. Sixth, some states require
forclosure regardless.
In certain states, if a buyer has been
making payments for a certain period of
time, say five years, or if they've paid
a certain percentage of the purchase
price, say 20%, you have to go through a
full foreclosure process to get the
property back. You can't just cancel the
contract. So, you end up with all the
hassle and expense of foreclosure
anyway, but with the additional
complications of a land contract.
Seventh, memorandums cloud title. In
some states, you have to file a
memorandum of the land contract to
protect your interest and the buyer's
interest. This memorandum shows up on
title and can create issues down the
road, especially if there are disputes
about the contract terms or if the buyer
defaults.
Eighth, upset buyers can file leans. If
you take the property back from a buyer
under a land contract and that buyer is
upset about it, they can file leans or
clouds on the title that you then have
to litigate to clear before you can
resell the property. This creates
massive additional legal expenses and
delays.
These problems aren't theoretical. I've
seen every single one of them happen to
investors who thought land contracts
were simpler. They're not simpler.
They're more complicated and more risky.
Now, let me explain why using a
promisary note with a deed of trust or
mortgage solves all these problems.
First, the property deeds to the buyer
closing. This means clean title transfer
right away. The buyer is the legal owner
and you're not liable for what happens
on the property because you don't own it
anymore.
Second, you have a clear foreclosure
process in all states. Every state has a
wellestablished procedure for
foreclosing on mortgages and deeds of
trust. The law is clear, the process is
predictable, and attorneys know how to
handle it. There's no ambiguity about
what you need to do if the buyer stops
paying.
Third, you've better legal protections.
Mortgages and deeds of trust have been
around for centuries. The law is clear
and well-developed.
You have strong protections as a lender.
Fourth, it's much more attractive to
note buyers. When I evaluate whether to
buy a note, I strongly prefer notes
secured by deeds of trust or mortgages.
They're cleaner, easier to understand,
and easier to foreclose if necessary.
I'll pay much more for a note with a
mortgage than I will for a land contract
if I buy the land contract at all.
Fifth, buyers prefer owning the property
immediately.
Most buyers want to own the property,
not just have a contract to purchase it
someday.
When you tell them the property will
deed to them at closing, they're more
excited about the transaction. Six, no
ongoing liability for you. Once you
close and the property deeds to the
buyer, you're done with the property
ownership. You hold a lean, but you're
not the owner. You don't need liability
insurance. You're not responsible for
property taxes or maintenance. It's
clean.
The bottom line is this. Notes and
mortgages are simpler, cleaner, better
protected legally, and much more
marketable if you want to sell the note.
Let me emphasize this one more time
because it's critical. If you want to
sell your notes to me or any other note
buyer, you need to use promisory notes
with deeds of trust or mortgages. I have
no interest in buying land contracts.
They're more work, more risk, and more
complicated. I'll pay significantly less
for a land contract than I will for a
properly structured note and mortgage.
If you use land contracts, you're making
your notes much harder to sell and much
less valuable. You're leaving money on
the table. Don't do that. Use the right
legal structure from the start.
Remember, always use a promisory note
with a deed of trust or mortgage. Never
use land contracts. The property should
deed to the buyer at closing and you
should hold a lean through the deed of
trust or mortgage. This protects you,
makes the note more valuable, and
creates a clean, simple legal structure.
In the next module, we'll talk about
which properties qualify for seller
financing and which ones you should
avoid. Let's keep going.

metadata.shortDescription:
FREE Financial Analysis Fundamentals Course: https://www.realestatefinanceacademy.com/finance-prerequisite
Free Commercial Loan Document Kit: https://www.realestatefinanceacademy.com/commercial-loan-document-kit/
—
A promissory note is the document used to show the evidence of debt in the case of a loan and the promise on the part of the borrower to repay the loan and the conditions under which those repayments are made.

Important to note is that typically loans are made with recourse. And recourse means that the borrower is personally liable for the total amount of the debt, regardless of whether or not there is enough security or collateral to cover that debt in the event of foreclosure. Sometimes loans can be what's called non-recourse in which case is only the collateral that is used to cover the debt in case of default. But that would need to be specifically defined in the loan documents.

As the loan is being paid down, the amount that is left to be repaid is typically called the unpaid principal balance.

Most often loans are advanced with all of the principal loan to the borrower upfront, but that's not always the case. There are other types of loans, like construction loans, lines of credit where advances can be made incrementally or in separate parts. 

The interest rate is the costs that the borrower pays to the lender for the use of their funds. The interest rate is expressed in annual terms such as 6% per year. And the interest rate can be either fixed or adjustable depending on the type of loan that's being made.

Monthly or annual payments - The promissory note will designate the number of payments, the amount of the payments and the date on which each payment is due. Whether it be monthly annually, quarterly, what have you.

Application of payments- Payments can be put towards interest, principal fees and other items. The promissory note will designate in what order those payments are applied. Typically in real estate, we see payments are applied to any outstanding fees, then interest, and then whatever's left over is applied to the principal.

Maturity date determines the term of the loan or the length of the loan and the maturity date is the date on which all unpaid principal balance is due. 

Along with the maturity date is the amortization quite often the amortization and the term of the loan are the same, say 30 years, but not always. Sometimes the term of the loan will be shorter, but payments will be amortized over a longer period. In that case, we end up with a balloon payment at the end. 

Collateral - Usually in real estate, this is accompanied by a mortgage document or a deed of trust that links the promissory note and the collateral together in the event of default, the lender can Sue on the note and foreclose on the mortgage going after the security or the collateral at the same time.

Default is when the terms of the note have been violated by either non-payment or what we call technical default. When say the borrower doesn't maintain the property to the appropriate levels or fails to pay their property taxes. When default happens, the lender issues a notice of default and invokes what they call the acceleration clause. And that means that all amounts that are payable are now due. This is usually the first step in the process on the way to foreclosure.

Prepayment, or paying a loan off early, is considered a privilege, not a right. Lenders make loans for the purpose of earning interest on the money they lend, and if a loan is repaid early, the lender is not able to make the yield that they were expecting. A prepayment penalty is if a loan is paid off early. It can be a step-down penalty as a percentage of the unpaid balance. Or other formulas such as yield maintenance or defeasance. 

Assumability clause is the ability for the borrower to substitute another borrower in their place. The loan will have provisions in there for what must be done for a new borrower to assume the loan. 
There's also, what's typically called an assumption fee, which is similar to an application or a written origination fee and not the new borrower who is trying to assume the loan will pay a fee to the lender in order to process the loan assumption.

metadata.title: How Private Lenders Protect Their Money: Notes, Liens & Insurance
metadata.author: The Real Estate Lender
metadata.shortDescription:
How private lenders protect their money — the documents, in order. A private loan stands on three legs: the promissory note (the promise), the recorded lien (the security), and the verification stack (title search, a lender's title policy, and insurance with the lender named). This lesson builds each one, runs one complete worked example three ways, opens the three insurance gaps nobody reads, and shows how a loan ends — in default and in payoff — on paper.

Which page of the file do you think gets skipped most? Tell me in the comments.

00:20 The note, the lien, the title policy — the map
00:34 The three legs of a protected loan
00:59 Leg one: the promissory note
01:26 Why a promise is not a position
01:48 Leg two: the deed of trust
02:13 Recording: the stamp that sets priority
02:45 First position — and what stands ahead of it
03:09 The title search: reading the property's past
03:31 The lender's title policy
03:57 The worked example: one deal on paper (hypothetical)

metadata.title: Transactional Funding How Long Can You Use It?|Real Estate Investing|Best|Lending|lender|Fl
metadata.author: LearnREInvesting
metadata.shortDescription:
How long can you use Transactional Funding ?
https://besttransactionalfunding.com
Is there a time limit when using transactional funding?

 Transactional funding or transactional financing is defined by the length of time the investor needs money for the "transaction" to be completed. In some states the closing agents escrow both sides of the closing until all the documents and money are in place and then and only then will they complete the transfer of the deed to the property. If the closing requires court orders or city inspections, these closings can be delayed for days or even months.

The transactional funder should not have his money sitting in escrow all this time but rather wire in the money only on the day of the final closing. Transactional funding is often referred to as Flash Funding or One-day Funding because the actual time period of this private real estate financing should be only minutes or hours.

The transactional funding is used between the time the original property seller signs all the documents he is required to sign (HUD-1 Closing Statement, Deed, Bill of Sale (optional) and any additional documents required by the closing agent) and the time the end-buyer signs his required documents (HUD-1, Hold Harmless Agreement, or other documents as required by the closing agent).

There are transactional funding lenders who advertise 30, 60 and even 90 day transactional funding. In actuality, these extended time periods are actually not transactional funding because the lender charges points and interest for the "extended" time period. Transactional funding only has points and ancillary fees attached to borrowing it.

A "point" is actually one percentage point of interest. For example, if the transactional funder lends $100,000 for the transaction and charges two points, he will receive, $100,000 x 2% = $2,000 as his cost for lending the money. This expense is a cost of doing business and is tax deductible as such to the investor and ordinary income to the transactional lender. Remember, without the transactional funding, the investor would not be able to do this deal and would have made no profit what-so-ever!

Free REI Training 👉 https://youtu.be/MU_hBMGEPTs

Full Double Close Walkthrough 👉 https://youtu.be/Ebnjlq4AkW4

How much does transactional funding really cost, and what do lenders need to see before they fund your double close? This video breaks down transactional funding for real estate wholesalers using a labeled example deal, walks through what funders check before they wire, and covers the red flags that should make you walk away from a funder.

Transactional funding is short-term money that pays for your A to B closing when you buy from the seller, then gets paid back from your B to C closing when you sell to your end buyer, usually on the same day at the same title company or closing attorney. It often covers the full purchase price, which is how wholesalers double close without using their own cash.

On the example deal, a $150,000 purchase and a $185,000 sale, an example 1.5% funding fee comes to $2,250 plus two sets of closing costs. You'll also see the setup mistake that pushes that same example to 2.5% and costs an extra $1,500, plus when a double close is worth paying for instead of an assignment, like no-assignment clauses on bank owned, REO and short sale deals.

From there it covers transactional funding requirements, why most funders don't check your credit or income, how to protect your earnest money if the deal falls apart, the FHA 90 day resale rule, and the most common questions wholesalers ask about double closing. Fees and terms change, so check the double close funding link above for the most up-to-date terms and pricing. Costs shown are examples only and vary by funder.

metadata.shortDescription:
Depending on the transaction you're in, the escrow timeframe may vary. Some escrow might take 10 days, 17 days, 30, 60, 90 days..

However, on average, escrow takes about 30 days, and we're going to be talking about a typical 30-day escrow...

SO....
👉🏻 You've opened escrow! What do you do?

You want to make sure you have a realtor you can count on and that you're guided properly.

🚩The First 3 Days of Escrow
Buyer: Makes Earnest Money Deposit (EMD)
Lender: Starts processing loan to get you qualified for the loan

*Before escrow, you are only PRE-APPROVED for the loan.

🚩 Day 1-7:
Buyer: 
A) You will receive a Seller Disclosure 
Seller disclosure shows what has been changed or modified with the property. 
Make sure to go through this with your real estate agent so you could understand it.

B)You are entitled to get your own insurance quote.
Make sure you do your inspection, this is your responsibility as a buyer.

C) Escrow instructions

🚩Day 7-17:
Buyer: Negotiate for repairs and closing cost! You are not obligated to keep moving forward. This is where you want to make sure whether you want to keep to property or cancel.

🚩After Day 17:
The seller has the right to keep your Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) as liquidated damages.

👉🏻 You've negotiated your repairs, you've done your inspection.
Now you're ready to submit your removal of inspection contingencies!

🚩 By Day 21:
Buyer: 
A) Make sure you have your loan approval.
B) Keep in constant communication with your realtor and your lender, that any documents they need are turned in ON TIME, so they can make sure you're qualified by Day 21.

🚩 Day 25 :
Do your final walkthrough of the property. 

🚩 Day 29:
A) Finished loan signing. 
B) Escrow sent you your final number. 
- Fund the transaction: where the lender and escrow officer is going to fund and disperse the money where it needs to go: your agent, bank, closing cost etc.

🚩 Day 30:
Deed gets recorded under your name.
Once the deed is recorded, you will receive your key from your agent!

🔥 Congratulations, you officially own the home!
