metadata.title: Real Estate Wire Fraud: How to Protect Your Down Payment Before Closing
metadata.author: Katherine Brough
metadata.shortDescription:
Imagine saving for years to buy a home, only to lose your down payment to a real estate wire scam. Unfortunately, wire fraud is a serious risk during the homebuying process, and fraudulent emails can look almost identical to legitimate messages from your escrow company.

In this video, I explain how real estate wire fraud works, how to verify wiring instructions before sending your closing funds, and what to do if you suspect you've been scammed.

**In this video, you'll learn:**
- How scammers impersonate escrow officers, lenders, and real estate professionals
- Why fraudulent wiring instructions can look completely legitimate
- How to safely verify escrow wiring instructions
- Warning signs of real estate wire fraud
- What to do after sending your down payment or closing funds
- Steps to take immediately if you accidentally wire money to a scammer
- How sellers can protect their proceeds from wire fraud

**The most important takeaway:** Never rely solely on an email to verify wiring instructions. Always call your escrow officer using an independently verified phone number before transferring money.

If you suspect wire fraud, contact your bank immediately and report the incident to the FBI at https://www.ic3.gov.

Whether you're buying your first home, purchasing another property, or preparing to sell a home in Orange County, understanding these scams can help protect your money.

🏡 **About Katherine Brough**

Katherine Brough | Realtor®  
714 595 4334
Seven Gables Real Estate  
Serving Orange County, California

Subscribe for practical advice on buying, selling, and owning real estate in Orange County.

If you found this video helpful, please like, subscribe, and share it with someone preparing to buy or sell a home.

segments.text: Picking a loan type can feel confusing
when you're new. Do you go transactional
funding, hard money, or a DSCR loan? In
the next few minutes, I'll give you a
simple, highle way to think about each
one.
Before we dive in, please give this
video a thumbs up and hit subscribe so
you don't miss future breakdowns on real
estate funding basics.
Let's start with transactional funding.
This is generally used for double closes
in wholesaling. You contract a property
with the seller, then resell to your end
buyer, often the same day. A
transactional funding partner covers the
first closing and is repaid immediately
at the second closing. Fees are
typically a small percentage and are
paid out at closing, so it's important
that your deal has enough spread to
cover costs.
Now, hard money loans. These are
commonly used for fix and flip projects.
A lender may fund a portion of the
purchase and a portion of the renovation
budget. Costs are usually higher than
traditional loans, and many loans are
interest only for a short term. You'll
usually need a down payment, money for
construction draws, and reserves for
holding costs.
Next, DSCR loans, which stands for debt
service coverage ratio. These are most
often used for rental properties.
Instead of focusing on your personal
income, the lender looks at whether the
property's rent can cover the projected
mortgage payment with cushion. Many
investors use DSCR loans to scale
rentals because the qualification
focuses on the property's income

Usury is one of those topics most investors and private lenders don’t think about… until it becomes a problem. And once it’s a problem, it can get expensive fast.

Are you a private mortgage lender in California and want to make sure you’re not violating the state’s usury laws? In this video, we’ll cover the maximum interest rate that can be charged to a borrower, the exceptions to the usury rules, and a few things that unlicensed lenders need to know to stay compliant with the usury laws. metadata.title: How Usury & Other Consumer Lending Regulations Can Affect Litigation Finance Agreements
metadata.author: TownCenter Partners Litigation Finance
metadata.shortDescription:
Every state has usury laws that limit the amount of interest that a lender can charge a borrower.  
Because litigation financing is often misapprehended as a “lawsuit loan,” there has been some suggestion that usury law can apply to limit the return that funders can seek for their investment in a litigation matter.  But when the actual nature of a litigation funding transaction is properly understood, it becomes clear why usury law has no application to litigation finance.

https://app.contentsamurai.com/cc/87096

What Is Transactional funding and how it works! Transactional funding is the action where moneys are short term borrowed for the buying of varied types of properties that typiclly will be exchanged the same day.  For real estate investing, the best transactional funding is to use the temporary money for a short time (few hours) to buy a real estate investment property that we have already resold to another buyer.

Transactional funding is when these borrowed funds are that is bank transfered electronically to the closing title company representative who will be finalizing a double closing of the two properties on the same day.  It is of utmost importance that the monies are in place by the transactional lender and the final-buyer be put into the title company representative's escrow account from electronically wired funds only.

The utmost importance of electronic transfered monies can't be imposed enough because frauded money orders and cashier's checks are easly reproduced on todays copiers.  Transactional funding can not be cash funds for the purchasing of properties as closing attorneys or agents don't want to be given the responsibility of the monies. 

The legality is any person sending a large cash deposit must leave their social security number with different banks.  If they use their own account, their social security number is already on file and the large deposit information is sent to the IRS by law.

 Real Estate Investors use transactional funding to do real estate investment deals without using any money out of pocket. These transactional funding lenders only need to check the closing documents for both the buying and selling of the properties and check the final-buyer's money transfers are in the correct escrow account. 
 
When the transactional funding lenders are convinced everything is ready, he authorizes the go ahead on the closing.
  
Once the original seller has signed all his closing documents, the investor has signed his seller's documents and his end-buyer's documents, the transactional funder's money will be used to fund the first closing and the second closing with be funded with the end-buyer's money all within a few minutes. Final step, the transactional funding  lender's funds are transfered to their original financial institution. Payroll is due and you need to restock inventory for the weekend rush. have the money, technically, but it's locked up in a massive client invoice that won't clear for another 30 days. A traditional term loan is the wrong tool for a 30-day gap. When you take out a standard loan, you receive a massive lump sum upfront and you start paying interest on every single dollar immediately, regardless of whether you've spent it yet. A business credit card falls short here too. The credit limits are usually too low to handle major expenses and you generally cannot use a credit card to run employee direct deposits. This is the specific problem a business line of credit is built to solve. It gives you a flexible pool of cash that you can draw from on demand and that money deposits directly into your business checking account to cover immediate bills. It acts as a financial shock absorber. It prevents routine timing delays from destroying a healthy operation. Before you can pull cash from a line of credit, a lender has to approve you for a maximum limit based on your historical risk profile. Underwriters measure three main pillars to set that limit. Your personal credit score, your total time in business, and your average monthly revenue. Entry-level online lenders set the bar fairly low. They will often grant you access with just 6 to 12 months of operational history and a personal credit score around 625. Traditional banks require a much safer profile. To get a bank line, they typically demand two or more years of steady history and a strong credit score of 680 or higher. There is a strict rule in business lending. The harder to pass the underwriting barrier, the less you pay for the money. Take a look at this chart representing a $50,000 credit limit. Out of that total available pool, we are highlighting exactly $20,000, the precise amount you draw cover your immediate payroll. The primary cost advantage here is that you only pay interest on the active $20,000 draw. Holding that remaining $30,000 in reserve costs you absolutely nothing. If you take this $20,000 draw from a traditional bank and pay it back over a 6-month term, the bank uses a prime rate plus a margin formula. That keeps your total interest cost to roughly $583. Online lenders use different pricing models like simple interest or flat monthly fees. For the exact same $20,000 draw over 6 months, your cost could jump to $1,800 or even a staggering $3,488. The flat fee model is a mathematical trap. A lender might charge what sounds like a tiny 1.55% monthly fee, but because they charge that percentage on the original balance every single month as you pay it down, it translates to an annual percentage rate of roughly 31%. This brings us to the repayment phase and the revolving mechanic. A standard term loan permanently disappears as you pay it down, but with a line of credit, the money loops right back into your account. Every dollar of principal you pay back immediately refills your available credit. metadata.author: David Olds REI
metadata.shortDescription:
Hey there, it's David Olds REI, your full-time real estate investor from Chattanooga, Tennessee. My mission is to help you become a real estate millionaire, and today, let's dive into a question I received on YouTube about the difference between an assignment and a double close. I've been in the game for over two decades, with full-time experience since June 2009. I've closed over 1,500 wholesale deals, tackled dozens of rehabs, and acquired over 100 rental properties.

Now, when it comes to wholesaling, it's usually done through an assignment of contract. Here's the breakdown: you find a seller, let's say Mrs. Smith, with a property, and you contract it for $100,000. Now, you have the option to either close on the property for $100,000 and become the new owner, or you can sell the contract to an end buyer, and they close on it. The difference between your contracted price and the closing price with the end buyer is your assignment fee, and it goes directly to you at closing.

Let's say you contracted at $100,000 and sell the contract to the end buyer for $120,000. The $20,000 difference is your assignment fee, handed to you by the title company at closing. It's a straightforward process.

Alternatively, instead of assigning the contract, you can close on it and become the owner. In this case, you'll incur additional closing costs, perhaps bringing your total cost to $106,000. If you then sell it to your end buyer for $120,000, deducting your costs, your profit is $14,000. The key difference here is that it involves two transactions – A to B, and then B to C – resulting in slightly less profit due to additional closing costs.

So, when would you consider a double close? There are a couple of scenarios. Firstly, if your seller has to close by a certain date, but your buyer can't close until later. In this case, you might need to close on it using your own or someone else's money and then resell it to your buyer. The second scenario is when your assignment fee is substantial, like $100,000. In this case, you might opt for a double close to keep the assignment fee confidential from your buyer.

Most of the time, for fees up to $100,000, an assignment suffices. Ensure you have the correct paperwork to make it work smoothly. Remember, the only entity that may lose out in an assignment is the title company.

I hope this clarifies the difference between assignment and double close. If it did, hit the like, subscribe, and notification buttons. Stay tuned for more real estate insights. See you on the next one! 🚀💰 #WholesalingWisdom #RealEstateStrategies #DavidOldsREITalks"

metadata.title: Assignment of Contract Or Double Closing For Wholesaling
metadata.author: Lex Levinrad Real Estate Training and Coaching
metadata.shortDescription:
ASSIGNMENT OF CONTRACT OR DOUBLE CLOSING FOR WHOLESALING

Sample Assignment of Contract Form: https://www.lexlevinrad.com/assignment/ 

In this video, I talk about assignment of contract versus double closing and the advantages and disadvantages of each method. If you are a new real estate investor who is just starting to learn about wholesaling and flipping properties, then you should learn how to utilize both strategies. 

Assigning a contract for a fee allows wholesalers to "flip" properties without ever closing on them. Assigning a contract to someone else in exchange for an assignment fee allows the wholesaler to profit from flipping the contract to another buyer. That buyer then closes on the property and the wholesaler gets paid their assignment fee at the closing. 

In order to make a purchase contract assignable you need to put the words "and or assigns" on the purchase contract after the buyer's name. For example if the buyer is Jack Smith then on the purchase contract you would put "Jack Smith and or Assigns". This makes the contract assignable. 

If you are using a standard purchase contract for your State, then there is also a check box on the contract that you will need to check off that says "this contract may be assigned". 

The 3 main advantages of using the assignment of contract strategy when wholesaling are:

1. You do not need to pay any closing costs
2. You do not need to show up at the closing
3. You do not need to put up any money 

The only money that you will need to put up is the deposit in escrow which can be as little as $10 and which will be returned to you at closing. 

Assigning contracts allows wholesalers to potentially have a "Laptop Lifestyle" since they can theoretically be anywhere in the world when the closing happens. They get paid with their assignment fee which is wired from the Title Company to their bank account. This is a huge benefit because if a closing is delayed and the wholesaler is planning on travelling their plans are not delayed. If the wholesaler works remotely or even out of the country it makes no difference since they are not required to be at the closing. 

When would you not want to use an assignment of contract? If you are buying a property from a bank then you cannot use an assignable contract since the bank will not allow this. That means you cannot use the assignment of contract with any foreclosure, short sale or bank owned property (REO).

If you are buying from an online auction site like Hubzu.com or Auction.com you can also not use an assignment of contract since they will not allow it. And if you are buying from Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac or HUD you cannot use an assignable contract either.

So if you want to wholesale or flip a property that is bank owned, listed on an auction site or owned by a government entity then you will have to utilize the double close strategy. This means you will need to first purchase the property, and only once you own it, will you be able to resell it for a profit. 

The disadvantage of a double closing is you DO need to be present at the closing to sign the closing documents for both the purchase and the sale (two closings). Another disadvantage is you need to pay both closing costs for the purchase and the sale which will significantly cut into your profit. 

The third disadvantage is you will need to pay cash to buy the property before you can resell it for a profit. If you don't have the cash then you will need to use a Transactional Funding Company which will charge you a transactional funding fee which will cut further into your profits. 

The decision of when to use an assignment of contract versus a double close is relatively easy. If you are buying an off market property directly from a seller then ALWAYS use an assignable contract. If your profit is ridiculously huge, then consider double closing instead of assigning if you are concerned that your end buyer will think you are making too much. 

If you are buying from a bank, online auction site or government entity like HUD then you will always have to double close and will not be able to make the contract assignable since the banks will not allow this.

Disclaimer:  
    
The information in this video and in the text above does not, and is not intended to, constitute legal advice; instead, all information in this video are for general informational and educational purposes only. Please consult with a real estate attorney in your State to obtain advice with respect to creating and using purchase contracts. I highly recommend you have an attorney create a purchase contract and assignment contract for you specifically for your use in your State. 

If you would like to see a sample Assignment of Contract please visit https://www.lexlevinrad.com/assignment/

metadata.author: House Math
metadata.shortDescription:
Sam just made his very last mortgage payment. No more bank, no more loan. The house is finally his… or is it?

Even with your mortgage paid off, there's still someone who can take your house, and it isn't the bank. In this video, we follow Sam step by step as his property tax bills go unpaid, from penalties and interest to a tax lien, a tax sale, and the last chance to save his home.

You'll learn:
• Why escrow quietly paid your property taxes and insurance, and what changes when the loan ends
• How penalties, interest and a tax lien pile up
• The difference between a tax lien sale and a tax deed sale
• What the redemption period is, and why it matters
• What happens to the extra money if your home is sold at a tax sale
• How to build your own "escrow" so this never happens to you
• Where to get help: payment plans, homestead exemptions and appeals

0:09 Sam's last mortgage payment
0:24 What escrow was secretly paying
0:44 What property tax actually is
0:58 The bill goes in the pile
1:08 Penalties and interest
1:16 The tax lien
1:32 Notice after notice
1:39 The county gets ready to sell
1:48 Tax lien sale vs. tax sale
2:02 The redemption period
2:18 Losing the deed
2:28 What happens to the extra money
2:51 How Sam saves his house
3:07 Insurance and HOA dues
3:24 Build your own escrow
3:37 Where to get help
3:57 The answer
4:06 Next: Frank's house
4:16 Rules vary by state

These are example numbers. Rules on property taxes, liens and tax sales are different in every state and county. This video is for general information only and is not legal, tax or financial advice. Check with your local tax office before you decide anything.

metadata.title: Who Pays Closing Costs in Florida? Buyer vs Seller Breakdown (Full Guide)
metadata.author: Suzanne & Chad Team: CPA + Realtors

0:00 Wondering who pays what at closing in a Florida real estate deal? 
Whether you're buying or selling, this video breaks down all the typical closing costs — including which party usually covers each item, what’s negotiable, and what to watch out for.

Skip the confusion and get the clarity you need before signing a contract!

💰 Seller Typically Pays For:

0:36 ✅ Agent commissions (usually 5–6%)
1:25 ✅ Owner’s title insurance (county-dependent)
2:17 ✅ Documentary stamp tax on the deed (70¢ per $100)
2:52 ✅ HOA estoppel certificate (if in an HOA)
3:39 ✅ Municipal lien search
4:04 ✅ Any unpaid property taxes (prorated at closing)
4:26 ✅ Mortgage payoff (not a closing cost, but due at closing)
4:42 ✅ Seller’s portion of title company fees

🏡 Buyer Typically Pays For:

6:09 ✅ Loan-related fees (points, origination, underwriting)
6:23 ✅ Escrow prepaids (insurance and property taxes)
6:32 ✅ Appraisal and inspections (usually paid before closing)
7:10 ✅ Brokerage fees
7:35 ✅ Prorated property taxes and HOA dues

📌 BONUS TIPS:

7:51 ✅ Always ask your agent for a seller net sheet or buyer estimate
8:12 ✅ Choose a lender who gives a detailed loan estimate, not just a rate

🎯 Whether you're buying your first home or selling your tenth, this info will save you money and headaches.

🔔 Subscribe for more expert real estate breakdowns and local market tips!

📞 954-304-4932

metadata.shortDescription: A buyer arrives ready to close, confident that the cash-to-close amount is settled, then notices unfamiliar property-tax and HOA adjustments on the settlement statement. The numbers are not necessarily wrong, but nobody has clearly explained who is paying for which days, bills, or special assessments. Matthew uses this real-world escrow surprise to make prorations understandable without burying listeners in legal or accounting jargon. The episode delivers three practical lessons: how to compare the latest settlement statement with earlier estimates, how to distinguish routine prorations from unpaid balances or special assessments, and which questions to ask the escrow officer, lender, agent, and HOA before signing. Buyers learn how to budget for post-closing bills, while sellers learn how inaccurate records or undisclosed assessments can delay completion. The episode ends with a simple line-by-line review habit listeners can use on any settlement statement before money changes hands.

metadata.title: Property Taxes at Closing in Oregon | What are Prorations, Escrow Deposits, Hold & Pay?
metadata.author: Julee Felsman | Workshop Team | Guaranteed Rate
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, you’ll learn what you’ll pay in property taxes when you close on a home purchase in Oregon. It’s more than you might realize – and more importantly, it’s more than your lender might realize. If, as is often the case, your lender doesn’t estimate property taxes accurately, you could have an unexpected and unwelcome surprise – more money due at closing that you’d budgeted to pay. 

So watch this video and you’ll learn about the three elements of property taxes that are due at closing in Oregon: prorations between you and the seller, escrow deposits with your lender and (if you close in September or early October) a “hold and pay”. I’ll even show you where to look on your Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure to find each item and verify the amounts shown are correct. 

And because taxes in Oregon are a bit weird, this video is part of a playlist, devoted to all of the things you need to know about taxes while you shop for a home, at the time of closing and going forward as a homeowner. Check out all of the videos here: 

Have any questions or want to talk about your situation? Let's chat!

Join Molly Tennant, business partner and operations manager for Pace Morby, as she delves into the intricacies of a joint venture agreement. metadata.title: Hard Money Secrets: Scaling Your Real Estate Portfolio with Gabrial Carter
metadata.author: Beyond The Deals Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Join Gabrielle Simmons on the Beyond the Deals podcast as she sits down with Gabe Carter of Capital Fund 1 to discuss high-leverage financing for real estate investors. Gabe shares his journey from a corporate analyst to a full-time investor and now a direct hard money lender.12

What’s Inside:
- Direct Funding: Learn how Capital Fund 1 uses its own capital to fund fix-and-flips, ground-up construction, and rental properties.
- Fast Closures: Discover how to get funded in 24–48 hours with minimal documentation.
The "High Roller" Program: New details on aggressive leverage for experienced borrowers—up to 90% of purchase and 100% of rehab costs.
- Deal Feedback: Why a lender's "haircut" on your numbers can be the best reality check for your investment.
- Investor Connection: Gabe shares his goal of funding $150 million in loans this year and his open invitation to visit local investor projects.

Connect with Gabrial Carter:
Website: https://capitalfund1.com/
Email: gabrial@capitalfund1.com
Service Area: Multiple States- RE Dealmakers "Denver Designated"

Sponsor:
Builder Outlet: Your source for windows, cabinets, doors, and trim. Visit buildersoutletco.com.

Why YOU Should Become a Private Money Lender in 2025 | Top 5 Reasons

Tired of the headaches of tenants, toilets, and turnover? In this video, I break down the top 5 reasons you should become a private money lender in 2025. 

Discover how you can generate passive income, protect your capital, and free up your time without buying or managing properties.

Whether you're a busy professional, early retiree, or real estate investor ready to pivot, this video walks you through:

- What private money lending is and how it works
- Who private lending is best suited for
- 5 key questions to ask before becoming a private lender
- 4 lending strategies you can choose from—DIY, partnerships, placements, and debt funds
- How to match your goals with the right level of passivity, control, and risk tolerance

⭐️ LET'S WORK TOGETHER⭐️
🌐 https://lend2live.com/
💻 beth@flynnfamilylending.com

⭐️PURCHASE MY BOOK ON PRIVATE MONEY LENDING⭐️
https://lend2live.com/book/

⭐️ STAY CONNECTED WITH ME⭐️
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/@lend2live.beth

Who is Lend2Live Management?

Lend2Live Management LLC blends the deep expertise in real estate investment and private money loan origination offered by Matt Flynn and Beth Johnson of the Flynn Family Lending team with proven legal, fund management and operations provided by Gerard Figurelli and William Hsu, also known as the HsuperG LLC team.

Matt Flynn is the co-founder of Flynn Family Lending and has over 30 years’ experience in all aspects of real estate investing including wholesaling, flipping, value-add buy and hold investing, and private money lending. In 2014, he co-founded Flynn Family Lending with his wife, Beth Pinkley Johnson, offering creative financing solutions across WA state. Beth is the co-author of Lend to Live: Earn-Hassle Free, Passive Income in Real Estate with Private Money Lending, published in July 2022 by BiggerPockets.com and launched the Lend2Live brand to provide educational and investment opportunities to those interested in private money lending.

The Lend2Live team is comprised of Gerard Figurelli, a seasoned hedge fund manager and founder of Vector Partner LLC, a hedge fund and fund consultancy business, and William Hsu, Managing Shareholder at Oseran Hahn P.S. and a leading transactional attorney in the Pacific Northwest with experience in a variety of legal matters, including cross-border international transactions, business and tax planning, securities offerings, corporate governance, mergers and acquisitions, as well as real estate acquisitions, development, dispositions, financing, and leasing.

Together, the Lend2Live Management team brings over 100 years’ knowledge and experience in private money lending and real estate transactions, business strategy and operations, as well as financial and legal expertise. Our goal is to create and maintain a safe environment for your investments and to protect them as if they were our own.

And so lead generation, I'm not going to talk to you about the this classic whatever. I'm going to show you exactly what I do. And there's really four things that I've put into practice at different times, but I want to show you which are the most effective and why. So this is kind of the the core four breakdown that Alexi talks about. You can go one to one, you can go one to many, you can talk to people you know or people you don't. One to one being text messages, phone calls, whatever. So people you don't would be what's called cold outreach. This is what a lot of people spend way too much time focusing on because you're literally reaching out to people who don't know you, don't like you, don't trust you. People that you know onetoone again, text, DMs, phone calls, whatever. But this is warm outreach because they actually know you. This is people that might be in your contacts or a friend on Facebook, follower on Instagram, so on and so forth. People you don't know going one to many is going to be content. An example of speaking to people you don't know in a one to many setting would be this video right here. I'm talking to you guys. Hopefully at least more than one person ends up watching this video. And so this is one to many people. And then people you do know that can go on to many would be referrals. All right. Now, every one of these things comes in stages. And the thing that I did to build a $149,000 business month while I was traveling was focusing on these two stages right here. Referrals and content. Why? Well, we're going to talk about this even more later, but if we're looking at something that's one to one versus one to many, what's going to be more effective? Of course, it's going to be one to many. And the excuse that people always give me is, "Well, I don't have a big audience or followers or whatever. And look at me, guys. Neither do I. But it doesn't matter in a business where you can make so much money off of these deals because it doesn't take a million people. It just takes one to get started. And so what I focused on is the following with content. Yes, I get on screen like this and a few people watch these things. But the primary way that I'm bringing in deals is by looking for what I call the watering hole, which is really simple if you know what to look for. When I talk about the watering hole, what I'm saying is where are the people hanging out that I want to work with? Now, if you are working in the transactional funding space and you want to grow that business, then you're looking for wholesalers and buyers. And so, you need to figure out where are those people hanging out? What meetups are they going to? What Facebook and school groups are they a part of? And then you need to go into those places because you can borrow an audience. And so, when I started building this business, the content that I was really creating wasn't just a bunch of videos because I don't have a big following. The content I was creating was borrowing other people's followers by doing written posts inside of those groups. I'm literally borrowing other people's audiences. And if you're watching this right now, all you have to know how to do is draw people out. You don't have to have every piece of the puzzle. And so, when I was getting started, I didn't have a ton of money raised. I didn't have the perfect systems, whatever. I just started focusing on lead generation to get people coming in the door. That's step one. But step two, the real killer is referrals because this is when people start working for me almost like employees except I don't pay them until we make money. So I can have unlimited, right? I don't have any payroll on these people. And the promise to these referrals is simply, hey, you go find the deal, right? you go find the deal and then we'll partner and they'll bring the deal and I'll bring the systems. So that's the capital and you know the TC's, the contracts, all of that good stuff. And then we'll split that let's say 5050, right? It's a really good deal for the people that want to work with me because they're making 50% of the profit even though they're probably only doing like 5 to 10% of the work. So, it's a really good deal for them, but it can be a really good deal for me. Why? Because I go out and I find 1,000x the amount of people as I could be doing this on my own. And so then when I'm traveling on vacation doing these things, I have a thousand people that are out looking for deals for me that get as much if not more of a benefit as I do by actually going out and finding these deals, right? And so my fundamental pillar, the thing that most people don't focus on, and by the way, if you're not running a transactional funding business, this can translate to literally anything you're doing, you don't have enough leads. Not even close. And if you can find ways to amplify and multiply those leads without killing yourself from a time perspective, your business is going to grow 10 times faster because it no longer just relies on you. So that's number one. Number two, which by the way you can only get to once those leads start coming in. Until you have don't have anything else you're able to do, you need to focus on leads, right? Alex Ramosi says until your business is overflowing with leads, you should be spending 4 hours a day on leads. And he says that even for people that have full-time jobs, not necessarily saying that, but the point is it should be your primary focus. Stop focusing on things that might make you money at some point in the distant future and start focusing on the things that can make you money right now. And that's exactly what I did. I've done it for years. A lot of it behind the scenes. Most of it nobody has seen. And it pays off eventually because your outputs lag your inputs. You have to put in extra inputs now. If you want the outputs later, you expect to get those results in a week. That might mean it's going to take a month or a year. But if you know it's going to work, why the heck does it matter? Right? So lead generation is number one. Number two is systems. You don't need systems. You don't need fancy systems until what? Until you have leads. But once you have leads, you have to implement the systems. Because if I have 10 leads coming in a day, which is about what we're at right now, right? If we have 10 leads coming in a day, then each of the things I'm about to draw out has to happen 10 times. So 10 times we have to vet those leads, right? And then 10 times we have to sign contracts for those deals. And then for the capital, we're going to need to fund those deals, right? And let's say the average deal size is $250,000. Well, now we're going to need 10x that amount of capital, right? So, we're going to need systems in place for raising that money. And so on and so forth as the deal goes on. Everything is going to need to be systemized. And either you're going to do 10 times the work that you were doing, right? Which there is a cap on that. There's only 24 hours in a day you have to be able to function and there's a lot of other things that have to happen besides this. Or you can use systems and automation. This can be simple and it can grow exponentially, right? So basic systems that I put in place was things like having a website for people to go to, right? when they submit that deal. A basic system is having a CRM for the deal to go into for it to be reviewed. An advanced system is using something like an AI review tool that I've now built that can review those deals so that I don't have to necessarily review all of them. Right? So now we're reviewing them. We have automated contracts, right? We have a a deal portal for people to track their deals. All of these different things and many many more have been put into place to create these systems so that something that would be 10 times the amount of work is the same amount of work but more efficient which means we can bring in more people and of course make more money. And then the final thing with all of these systems being tied together is that somebody has to run these things. And if I'm going to be out traveling or if I'm going to be out trying to grow this business from a le perspective, then we're going to need a team to keep the ship afloat. And that's exactly what I have, right? I have an amazing team of people that help run the backend, that help coordinate, that get on phone calls, that do all of this stuff. And notice I'm talking about this stuff in order, right? Again, does any of this even matter if you don't have leads? Absolutely not. But the second thing that I focused on was systems to take those leads and convert them into more money. And once I was doing that, then I moved to the third and by far my favorite thing that I have done to grow to $149,000 a month. And that is focusing on leverage. Leverage is probably the coolest thing I've ever discovered in my life. I've told the story many times that back when I was getting started, I was funding $5,000 EMDs for real estate investors and I was charging about 20%. So, I was profiting $1,000. And after a few months of doing that, I decided I wanted to scale that to the moon. I had a bunch of leads. I had decent systems. And so, my goal was to do 30 deals in one month. And if everything had gone according to plan, which you can probably guess how that went, but if it had gone according to plan, I was going to profit $25,000 total off those 30 deals. Now, 30 deals means 30 people, 30 contracts, 30 title companies, 30 sellers, 30 buyers, right? All of this different stuff. It was absolutely insane. And of course, what ended up happening is I lost track of everything. Deals fell through. real estate happened. I ended up losing most of that money and of course not making this 25 grand right now. And I showed you guys at the beginning of this video on the screen. Now I go out and I'll fund a million dollar deal and that deal alone will profit 25 grand. Just did one of those the other day. Right. This right here is more money, but it's the exact same amount of work. It's the same contracts, but it's one person, one title company, one of everything. Right now, this is a dream scenario. And that's why it comes third because once you've nailed down your leads, once you've nailed down your systems, then the goal is how can I do the same amount of deals but get 10x, 50x, 100x the returns, right? This right here from this is 25x the returns for the same amount of effort. And once I started employing leverage, my business grew to where after that failed 25k a month, I was doing about 10k a month. And this was in March of 20, time flies, 2024, right? And by right now when I'm recording this video, or I'll just use the example I put up. So December of 25, we did $149,000 in a month and we did that with less deals, right? I it was 12 deals total to produce that kind of capital. How the three things that I've just talked about, those are the only three things that I have used. Now, there's a ton of things that don't matter or that you don't have to do in order to get here. You don't have to be famous. You don't have to have a big following. You don't have to go to every single dumb conference that you see people posting about. You don't need to sit in hours and hours of Zooms. You don't need to have a ton of your own money. You don't need to spend hours and hours and stay up late and wake up early every single day. You don't need to do all of those things that sound cool but don't necessarily move the needle. Because if you can just focus on these three things, you will build a successful business. I've seen it for my own business, but not just my own. I've seen it for tons of other people's businesses that I have worked with and helped scale. Because building a funding business is not about doing more. It's about getting more out of what you already do and knowing a strategy that you can employ in order to do that. So, that's how I had $149,000 month doing just three things and not focusing on a lot of the other BS that people talk about. And if you're watching this video and you want to build a business like that, first of all, it's not going to happen overnight, obviously. But it 100% can happen. If I can do it, you can do it. If other people can do it, you can do it. And if you are interested in building that business, I created a full free training how you can start from scratch and actually do that. It walks you through all of my lead generation tactics in depth. It's got a bunch of worksheets and quizzes and live trainings and everything else. And if you click the first link in the description, you can jump into that. It's called the Capital Club. You can get all of that stuff for free. I would love to see you inside of there.

Building a business in South Africa without family connections requires serious grit and humility. Real entrepreneurship often looks like credit card debt and small-town hustles before anyone calls you a success. Knowing when to walk away from what you built is just as vital.

#SouthAfricanEntrepreneurs #BlackBusinessSA #EntrepreneurshipJourney

Please note that The Conversation Capital and all of our content does not constitute professional advice of any kind. This includes, but is not limited to, financial, medical, legal, psychological, spiritual, or educational counsel.

We encourage our viewers/listeners to seek guidance from qualified professionals for any specific needs or concerns.

metadata.title: What is an ABC Closing and transactional funding usage.
metadata.author: LearnREInvesting
metadata.shortDescription:
See full written post here and more details about best transactional funding
https://besttransactionalfunding.com/

What is an A-B-C Closing in Real Estate?

As soon as I think I have seen it all something new pops up. 
When I do transactional funding for wholesale same-day double closings I meet literally hundreds of closing agents and closing attorneys across the country.  
Every once in a while, I have some interesting feedback about their closing practices.

Very often a new investor gets confused about the specifics of the closing cycle.
I can help because I have done thousands.  Investors are eager to listen and learn especially when they have serious profits at stake. If the closings don’t happen everyone from the investor to the end-buyer loses everything.

The closing agent should be the focal point of the transaction always working with all the parties to get the deal to close. Unfortunately, the actual people doing the closings may be paid hourly.
With little incentive to do more than is minimally required, the closing person can be set in his/her ways about how they are willing to do the double closings.  This is especially true if the investor isn’t familiar with the closing process and who funds what parts of the closing cycle.

Some of these closing agents are so set in their ways that they flat say “no” to practices that are very commonly done by other closing agents perhaps a few hundred yards away.

Being specific about what you want done in a double closing, assignment of contract or with a Joint Venture (“JV”) Agreement is critically important.  As an example, I had a new investor call me about transactional funding who needed the funds in two days.

My process is very simple, I have the investor send me the A – B and B – C signed contracts and then tell the closing agent to copy me on correspondence for the closing.
The reason for the copies of the purchase and sale contracts is to give me information that will be critical to the closing.
This includes the Seller, Buyer/Investor, the End-buyer, closing agent(s) and information about the property.
I then call the person doing the closing and explain that I will be funding 100% of the money due from the investor on the A – B leg and I get paid back from the B – C closing leg.

In this case the investor had contacted a closing agent she was referred to and said the closing would be an “A-B-C” transaction.
The closing agent responded that her attorney-owned firm could not legally do this type of closing and there were no exceptions.
This left the investor with having to do a double closing at two different closing agents which may be workable, but it can be risky for a transactional funder.
This problem of agents not wanting to do double closings is not uncommon and often misguided.
Double closings are important when the profit spread is large or secrecy of the sale by the investor is important.
Too large a profit is in “the eyes of the beholder” and can be $10,000 or greater depending on the sale price.
In some cases, I have seem sellers say they wouldn’t close because the investor was making too much and in one case this amount was only $2,500.
What I suggested to the investor was to switch the closings to another agent/attorney who does a huge volume of investor closings.
While the two-day deadline had to be extended the double closing went off without a hitch and all parties were very satisfied.
What happened that the one agent wouldn’t close the original transactions?
As I reviewed the email chain and talked with the investor, it was clear that the use of the term “A-B-C” closing meant something different to the agent.
One thing that every investor tries to do is use the end-buyer’s funds to fund his original purchase.
Without going into the legalities and actual practices, it is safe to say that most closing agents and title insurance companies do not allow these transactions.


I wish you limitless success in all you do,
Dave Dinkel

Can private money lending really replace your 9–5?

The real reason most people don’t get results

metadata.author: Kemedia
metadata.shortDescription:
What is Transactional Funding for Real Estate Wholesaling Properties?

For Funding: http://theborrowerschoice.com 

What is Transactional Funding? Transactional funding is a creative financing strategy often used by real estate wholesalers when conducting a double closing aka a simultaneous closing. Transactional funding is a short-term loan that is borrowed and paid back quickly, usually within the same day, and sometimes as long as a week. Access to this kind of short-term financing allows real estate wholesalers to buy and sell properties quickly without using any of their own money. Transactional funding is typically provided by a hard money lender or private money lender and is only used when there is an established and well-documented end buyer in place. This end buyer should be ready to buy the subject property from the wholesaler immediately after the wholesaler purchases the property from the original seller. Then the sale proceeds from the end buyer, are used to pay back the transactional funding loan. Here’s how transactional funding works. The wholesaler/investor finds a motivated seller and both parties agree to a below-market purchase price (the A-to-B transaction). When the wholesaler/investor finds an end-buyer, they will sign a new purchase agreement (the B-to-C transaction) to purchase the property at a higher price and close on the same day as the A-to-B transaction. The wholesaler/investor secures transactional funding to buy the property from the seller. When both transactions are complete, the wholesaler/investor repays the transactional funding loan from the proceeds of the B-to-C transaction and keeps the difference as their profit. metadata.title: E-Tender Escrow Explained | EMD Refunds in Govt Tenders (India)
metadata.author: Cash Management Simplified
metadata.shortDescription:
What is an e-tendering escrow and how does it keep bid money safe? When a government body runs an online tender, every bidder pays a participation fee and an earnest money deposit (EMD). An e-tendering escrow lets a neutral bank hold all that money until the tender closes and results are announced, then refund the EMD of unsuccessful bidders and settle the winner's EMD to the government body. In this explainer we follow three bidders on a road project tender to see the money come in, the results, and the refunds.

Quick answers:
• What is an e-tendering escrow? An escrow account that holds bidders' participation fees and EMDs for a government tender until the results are announced.
• What is EMD in a tender? Earnest money deposit: an amount each bidder pays to show they are serious about the bid.
• What happens to EMD if you lose a tender? In this arrangement, the bank refunds the full EMD to unsuccessful bidders after the tender is completed.
• What happens to the winner's EMD? It is settled to the government body's account.
• Why use an escrow for tenders? Bidders' money stays secure for the whole tender period, and refunds and settlements are handled transparently by the bank.

segments.text: In this video, I'm going to teach you
how to stack business credit cards the
right way without you ever having to
worry about getting denied again. Let's
begin. Okay, what is going on family?
Let's start off and address the biggest
question that exists, which is what
exactly is business credit card
stacking. So, by definition, stacking is
a process of creating a list of banks
strategically that allows for you to
apply for multiple business credit cards
at the same time so you can maximize
your approvals and minimize the amount
of hard inquiries on your report. very
important for us to know. Now, the
reason why this strategy is so important
and why it matters is because most
people when looking for funding, they're
applying for multiple business credit
cards, but they do so blindly. And as a
result, without them knowing it, they
may or may not be hurting their approval
if they are not careful with where these
credit report or excuse me, these credit
cards or these lenders are pulling from.
But when you stack strategically, you
allow yourself to create a structured
and protected way to get funding without
blasting your credit report with a bunch
of uh miscellaneous inquiries. So,
here's a visual example. I'm a visual
guy. I'm sure some of you guys at home
may be visual as well for you guys to
pretty much understand. Let's say you
have two people, person A and person B,
right? Both of these individuals are
going to go to three banks because they
want to get 50, 75, 100K in funding.
Cool. Person A is going to go to three
banks, but because he does not have a
funding sequence or because he didn't
stack, he doesn't not stacking
correctly. He's going to go to three
banks blindly without knowing that all
three of those banks pull from
TransUnion. The problem with that is
that by the time he goes to the first
bank, he's going to get a nice good
amount if all his stuff is together,
right? Personal credit, business credit,
and beyond. So, he's going to get his
little 25K. Whoopdedoo. By the time he
gets to the second bank, what happens is
this second bank here is going to see
that he got an inquiry from this first
bank. And if this second bank was going
to give him 25K, they've now decreased
it to 15K. Then he goes to this third
bank. Well, the third bank is going to
see inquiries one and two that just
happened. And they're going to say,
"Well, hold on. We were going to give
you 25, but it's very clear that you are
needy for credit. We don't trust you as
much. We're only going to give you
7.5K." So whether he knows it or not,
person A has just drastically decreased
his funding capability or funding
potential simply not by having the
proper business stacking business credit
stacking sequence in play. Versus if we
look at person B, they also go to three
banks, but this person has a funding
sequence or stacks correctly. He's going
to go to three banks, but he's going to
go to one that pulls Experian, one that
pulls TransUnion, and one that pulls
Equifax. And what this does is it not
only protects his credit report with
each of these credit reporting agencies,
but he can go to all three of these at
the same time and none of them is going
to know he went to the other bank cuz
they're all looking at three completely
different reports. So in turn, what it
does is it keeps his personal credit
report, the amount of inquiries on his
personal credit report minimal. It
maximizes how much capital he's able to
get access to. And person B is a very
happy person and person A, not so much.

person B. And this is exactly what that
process looks like in order for us to
make sure that we're stacking but doing
it correctly. The first thing that we
want to do is we want to make sure that
we have a foundation that is stackable,
right? We want to be able to stack on a
foundation that is that can handle it.
The first order of business is making
sure our personal credit is good. What
does that look like? That's no negative
items under 10% utilization. Some people
will say 30% or higher, but the thing is
that's that's okay. 30 staying at 30% is
okay, but 10% is actually is going to
help boost up your score. So, we want to
be at 10%. No more than two to three
hard inquiries. You want to have two
plus years of credit history. And here's
a good important one. You want to have
at least three to five plus cards with
5K plus limits. Fun fact, there's
something in the business credit space
called comparable credit. Pretty much
saying like, "Hey, when you're applying
for business credit at certain
locations, that lender is going to take
the limits on your personal credit cards
and use that in your decision-making for
how much they give you on the business
side." So, if all your credit cards have
$1,000 limits, do not be surprised, even
if you stack correctly, that you're
going you're out here getting 2,000,
$3,000, $4,000 approvals on the business
side because you haven't shown that you
can handle any more than that. So, there
you go. That's the personal credit
checklist. Now, the business structure
checklist is also pretty
straightforward, which is you want to
make sure you have your business name.

business EIN. You want to have your
operating agreement, your business
address, email, phone number, and
professional website. Why? Even if you
check off all these boxes here with the
personal credit checklist, right? If you
